They know that certain members of the last administration came into office poor and went out with the reputation of having many millions. I do not mean to accuse anyone in particular, but I can tell them that a great portion of the people of Canada thought that something was going wrong at the time and made it clear on the 21st of September last. The hon. member for Rouville paid a great compliment to the right hon. leader of the opposition in saying that in 1896 he had prevented a civil war; hut to-day hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to be afraid of war. This is why I suppose they are so quiet on the other side of the House on the school question. But, Sir, they have not always been as quiet as they are to-day. The hon. Postmaster General has accused the Liberal party of having played football with all the big questions that came before the parliament of Canada in order to obtain power. For my part, having known what was going on when I was with the Liberal party, I feel like pleading guilty. But what did the hon. member for Rouville answer? He read a letter from the Rev. Father Lacombe, and the answer of the 1554
right hon. leader of the opposition. The Massey hall speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition has already been referred to, so that I need not repeat it. Will you allow me to quote from * Hansard ' debates of the session of 1897, where I find that an hon. gentleman, before accepting the nomination for the county, I think, wihich the hon. Postmaster General represents, signed the following:-
Being sincerely disposed to put aside all party spirit and all questions of men, in order to secure the triumph of the Catholic cause in Manitoba, I, the undersigned, promise, if elected, to conform myself to the Bishops' mandement in all points and to vote for a measure according the Catholics of Manitoba that justice to which they have a right by virtue of the judgment of the Privy Council, provided that the measure be approved of by my bishop. I, the undersigned candidate in the county of Gaspe solemnly promise to vote in parliament in conformity with the desires of the R'ght Reverend Bishops as expressed in their last pastoral letter.

The right hon, leader of the opposition has been pleased to say on many occasions that Canada is a nation. What steps has the right hon. gentleman taken to give effect to that statement? Here again we see the game of football. But that is not all. But because I am convinced that the people of Keewatin, whether it be the majority or whether it be the minority will be protected to the fullest extent under article 22 of the present constitution of Manitoba.

I would like, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words in explanation of the vote I am about to give, not only on the amendment of my hon. friend from Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche), but also on the motion for the third reading of this Bill. My remarks will only bear upon one feature of this measure, that is on the omission by the government of a clause that will protect the rights and privileges in educational matters of the Roman Catholic population of Keewatin. My vote to-night will not differ from the one I have already given on the motion for the second reading of this Bill. It will not differ, Mr. Speaker, from the vote Mr. RAINVILLE.
I would have given on Tuesday afternoon on the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition had I been here. Sir, I will vote with the government. As my absence from the Capital when the question was put to the House may be misrepresented later on, and in hostile quarters, I -beg of you, though it be a personal matter, to allow me to explain. When I left Ottawa for Montreal on Friday afternoon on the first day of this month, I could not even suspect that the House would reach that phase in the progress of this Bill befope Thursday last. As a matter of fact, we all know that was the general belief; and confident that I would be here in time to take, by my vote, my full share of responsibility in the rejection of the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition, I spent four or five days of this month in Montreal, where my presence was called for by very urgent private and legal business. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, I was very disagreeably surprised when I reached Ottawa on Tuesday evening to hear that the vote had been taken. If anything could have alleviated my disappointment, it would have been that my determination to vote against the amendment of the leader of the opposition was very generally known. I approached this very important and troublesome problem with the earnest purpose that it should be solved in what I honestly believe to be the very best interests of all concerned. Sir, I have studied it with the greatest care in all its various aspects, taking into consideration all the circumstances and trying, as far as humanly possible, to put aside all influences of any kind whatever that could bias my judgment; and to-day, Sir, I have pleasure in realizing that I am in the best frame of mind and state of heart when I declare that I will stand by the government of the right hon. Mr. Borden. I truly believe this Bill to be the best measure that could be introduced here, under the actual circumstances, whether we look at it generally or from the special point of view of which I have mentioned. Though the question be much controverted as to whether the minority, in that part of Keewatin to be added to Manitoba, enjoys special rights and privileges in respect to educational matters, it seems to me to be now generally admitted that the provisions which apply are those of the Northwest Territories Act, chapter 62 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, which came into force on the 31st of July, 1907. The article X of chapter 62 of the above-mentioned statutes, reads as follows:
X. The -Commissioner in Council, if authorized to make ordinances respecting education, shall pass all necessary ordinances in respect thereto; but in the laws or ordinances relating to education it shall always be provided

that a majority of the ratepayers of any district or portion or subdivision thereof, by whatever name the same is known, may establish such schools therein as they think fit and make the necessary assessment and collection of rates therefor; and also that the minority of ratepayers therein, whether Protestant or Roman Catholics, may establish separate schools therein, and in such case the ratepayers establishing such Protestant or Roman Catholic separate schools shall he liable only to assessment of snch rates as they impose upon themselves in respect thereof.
Before that legislation could become operative, three conditions had to be reckoned with:
1st-That the government of this country should appoint a council of four members to assist the commissioner of the Territories.
2nd-That this Commissioner in Council should be authorized to make ordinances respecting education.
3rd-That this Commissioner in Council should make such ordinances.
Sir, we all know that up to the 10th of October, 1911, the very day this government came into power, none of these three conditions had been complied with. We all know that, as far as this government is concerned, the only demand ever received from the interested parties that the two first conditions above mentioned should materialize, reached the Governor in Council only on or about the 1st of December, 1911. In that respect, I fully concur with the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Borden):
I ask any honourable gentleman in this House whether or not it would have been a reasonable thing for that government, after that matter hod stood for nearly four years without the appointment of any council, without the authority of the commissioner to put into force these provisions respecting education. I would ask whether or not it would have been a reasonable thing for us to undertake to do that without which these Northwest Territories had got on very well for three and a half years at least. And, to do that, remember, on the very eve of carrying out a proposal to which parliament had given :ts unanimous acceptance on the 13th of July, 1908. Why, Mr. Speaker, I think it would have been the very worst thing we could do in the interests of all concerned if the government had seen fit on the eve of enlarging the boundaries of Manitoba, to take any such step as that which has been suggested.
But in view of the stand I am taking in this matter, the question whether or not separate schools are now in operation in Keewatin, according to article X of said chapter 62, has no importance whatever. I will even go farther and I will admit, for argument's sake, that these separate schools do exist to-day in Keewatin, according to that law. Have we the constitutional authority to force them to-day upon Manitoba? This question, Sir, has already been according to me, victoriously answered in the negative, by the right hon. leader of the government, one of the greatest legal minds we have to-day in Canada, and I do not know that this opinion of his has been yet contradicted, whether inside or outside of this House. I beg of you, Mr. Speaker, that I should be allowed to quote the right hon. gentleman's own words in that respect, as I humbly submit that I could not do as well as he has done himself:
I do not think it is constitutionally possible.
I would like to point out to hon. members, to whose attention this may not have been brought, that the provisions of the British North America Act of 1871, with regard to the constitution of the province in the first instance, are veTy different from those contained in the clause of the same Act, providing for the alteration of the boundaries of a province. Section 2 of that Act-the one which provided for the constitution of a province, carved out of the Northwest Territories, for instance, Alberta-reads as follows:-
The parliament of Canada may from time to time establish new provinces in any territories forming for the time being part of the Dominion of Canada, but not included in any province thereof, and may, at the time of such establishment, make provision for the constitution end administration of any suoli province, and for the passing of laws for the peace, order and good government of such province end for its representation in the said parliament.
But when we come to the third section of that statute-the one in virtue of which this Bill is brought before this House- we find that the language with regard to increasing the area of a province is in very different terms. It is as follows:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province of the said Dominion, increase, diminish, or otherwise alter the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions a9 may he agreed to by the said legislature, and may, with the like consent, make provision respecting the effect and operation of any snch increase or diminution or alteration of territory in .relation to any province affected thereby.
We have in the one section the direct authority of this parliament to deal with the constitution of a province. In the other section we have not any such thing, and it seemed, to me absolutely impossible to conceive that you can have a province in Canada, such as Manitoba would be after this Bill had passed, which would be governed as to one part of it by one constitutional provision in respect of education, and in another part of it, by another constitutional provision in respect of education. I do not believe that the British North America Act of 1871 contemplated any such thing. To my mind it is inconceivable, and I do not find warrant for it in the statute. It is inconceivable that yon could have one constitutional limitation in Manitoba and another constitutional limits-

tion in the part of Manitoba which we now propose to add.
Now, the right hon. leader of the government says that ' a proposal to place any such restriction upon Manitoba is politically impossible because,' he does * believe that Manitoba would not accept the extension of her boundaries coupled with any such restrictions.'
And later on the right hon. the Prime Minister adds that he is ' absolutely certain that it is politically impracticable.'
Well, Sir, I do not know of any other means by which this Bill could be amended so as to embody in it a clause safeguarding the rights and privileges mentioned in said clause X, whether this clause has been or not, to-day, taken advantage of. We have not the constitutional authority to insert that clause in this Bill without Manitoba's consent. And that consent, Manitoba is unwilling to give. We have the word of the right hon. gentleman to this effect. I am proud to say that I rely with the greatest confidence upon that affirmation. The right hon. gentleman who makes it is the man who, whilst he was touring the western provinces on the eve of the last federal election, said to the farmers who wanted him, as the leader of a great political party, to promise them reciprocity with the United States in natural products:
Gentlemen, I am against the reciprocity, and I would not make the promise you ask for, even if I knew that by doing it I would become the Prime Minister of this Dominion of ours.
Sir, the man who has the moral courage to speak in that way, in such circumstances, is not a Talleyrand, of such a man one cannot say that language has been given to him so that he might hide his thought.
And this is the reason why I say to-day that I believe the right hon. the Prime Minister, when he says that Manitoba is unwilling to ' accept the extension of her boundaries coupled with any such restrictions.' What are we to do then, Sir? Are we to say to Manitoba: All right, we shall keep Keewatin?
Where is the man that would dare to give such an advice to this government? We must not forget Mr. Speaker, that the honour of this House has been pledged to * a proposal to which parliament has given its unanimous acceptance on the 13th of July, 1908. We all know Sir, that, on the 12th of April, 1876, the district of Keewatin was made a distinct and separate district by chapter 21 of the statute of 1876, which statute came into force by proclamation of the Governor in Council on the 7th of October, 1876, and the reason given for that legislation by the legislator at the time was that Keewatin was to be made part of the province of Manitoba.
Mr. CODEBEE
Perusing lately the debates on this question in this House, I could not help noticing that a certain member took exception to that law being passed without a clause similar to clause X of chapter 49 of the Statutes of 1875, which chapter 49 is in force yet to-day, and gives a constitution to the Northwest Territories. That clause X of said chapter 49 of the law of 1875 is almost identically in the same terms as clause X of chapter 62 of the revised statutes of Canada:, 1906, which gives to the population of Keewatin the right to separate schools. I found then in the debates that the predecessors of the right hon. leader of the opposition, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, and the Hon. Edward Blake, then at the head of the Liberal party of the time and sitting in this House on the Treasury benches met that objection by saying that that omission of said clause X in the law of 1876 had been made purposely because in the course of time Keewatin or at least part of it, was to be added to Manitoba, and that the annexation would naturally and legally bring Keewatin in respect to educational matiers, under the law of the province of Manitoba.
What is the law one can find to-day in the province of Manitoba?
The law of 1890, passed by a Liberal government, and against the passing of which all the Conservative members of the legislative assembly, Protestants as well as Catholics, fought to the bitter end, a law which has deprived the minority in Manitoba of certain rights and privileges in respect to education according to a judgment of the highest tribunal of the empire. We know that that law of 1890 has been amended by the legislative assembly after the general election of 1896, which brought to power the right hon. the leader of the o position; but we know too, Sir, that this amendment, accepted by the right hon. leader of the opposition of to-day, then Prime Minister, does not give to the minority the full plenitude of their rights and privileges as admitted by that judgment of the Judicial Privy Council of the King. As a matter of fact, it is generally conceded, by all men of good faith at least, that was it not for the very generous and liberal interpretation given to that law of 1890 and its amendment by the Hon. Mr. Roblin, Conservative Premier of Manitoba, the position of the Roman Catholic minority in Manitoba to-day, though far from being what it should be, would be simply outrageous in the estimation of all broadminded and law-abiding men. What is the population in Keewatin to-day, Sir? In the territory there are at the present time not -more than 165 white people 400 or 500 half-breeds, and the balance of the population are Indians. The Roman Catholics, we are told, are in the minority. All rights and privileges are sacred to me,

Sir, but the rights and privileges of the few weak should be considered more sacred yet.
But, Sir, if by adopting that very dangerous and unwise device suggested to us that we should refuse to consent to the annexation of Keewatin to the province of Manitoba unless the representatives of( that province accept the incorporation in this Bill of a clause apt to safeguard and protect the rights and privileges of the few Roman Catholics of Keewatin, is it not to be feared that without bettering at all the actual position in educational matters of those Keewatin people, we would hurt the interests in that respect of the 250,000 Roman Catholics of Manitoba? Whai more human, Sir? The political agitation that would manifestly follow such a course in Manitoba in the whole of this Dominion, agitation influenced by the religious passion, the most dangerous of all in a mixed population like ours, would very naturally bring the people of Manitoba, who have been described to us by the right hon. leader of the government as * imbued with a big, broad, generous spirit, as inclined to deal with their fellow-countrymen who may be of a different faith in the same broad-minded and generous spirit as that which has been evinced in other provinces of Canada where no constitutional provisions of this kind exist,' such an agitation, I say, would very naturally bring them to retaliate on our Roman Catholic brothers in Manitoba, whose hopes for betterment in a near future and gain made in the past in respect to education, would then be lost.
Sir, this is my conviction, and1 that conviction is founded not only on human nature, but also on the experience gained during the years 1890 to 1897, on the very same matter, in the very same province. A great Canadian has said once: ' Let the country perish rather than a principle.' Sir, I do not belong to that school, and I refuse to-day to be coerced in saying: ' Let the 250,000 Roman Catholics in Manitoba perish if, to avoid that calamity it is necessary that the few hundreds of Roman Catholics in Keewatin should be placed not under the law passed in respect to education by the Liberal party of Manitoba in 1890, as amended in 1897 according to the poor settlement made that year by Messrs. Laurier and Greenway, a settlement which has been approved in this House by the hon. the member for Rou-ville to-day, then member for Gaspd, and by Mr. Henri Bourassa, then member for Labelle; no, sir, not under that law so miserably amended, but, Sir, under that law and its amendment as interpreted1 by the ' big, broad, generous spirit ' of the Hon. Mr. Roblin.
There is an agitation in my own native province, says the right hon. leader of
the opposition. We know it, Sir, and we know too that the right hon. gentleman in this House, is folding his arms, and is refusing to take any positive stand one way or the other in respect to this matter of school rights. He keeps cool and quiet, and he contents himself with putting before the House a double-faced amendment which will permit, on account of its vagueness and ambiguity, his political friends in the province of Quebec to say:	We are against that Bill because
there cannot be found in it a clause protecting the rights and privileges of the minority in Keewatin in respect of education and which will allow his partisan followers in the other provinces to say: We are against that Bill because some friends of the government wanted to coerce the province of Manitoba. We know too that the political organs of the right hon. gentleman in the province of Quebec are doing their best to bring that agitation to its greatest intensity. With respect to the agitation which is threatened to-day I would say to my hon. friends: Remember what we lost in 1896 in Manitoba through the agitation which' was aroused as far back as 1890, especially by the Liberal press and the Liberal politicians of that day; bear in mind what we have gained in the same province since the agitation has cooled down; do not forget what the right hon. leader of the government said lately as to the very refreshing state of things which exists in the province of Nova Scotia to-day because our Roman Catholic brethren there have never used that very dangerous weapon. See what the hon. member for Kent, N.B., (Mr. Robidoux) said yesterday to a reporter of the * Gazette,' a well known newspaper in Montreal, in respect to the happv lot in education matters of the Roman Catholics of New Brunswick who have always been careful not to agitate. Mr. Sneaker, I m'ght as well read this interview to the House:

Conditions are Satisfactory, Says Mr. Robidoux, M.P.
Mr. Robidoux, M.P. for the county of Kent, N. B., who was in the city on Saturday, made the statement that the general policy of the Borden government was giving satisfaction in the maritime provinces, and to the Acadian population in particular.	.
Mr. Robidoux is particularly well pleased wh' the immigration 'policy of the present government, as far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned. The hon. Mr. Rogers, he says, has just appointed Rev. Father Legace, of Legaceville, N.B., as immigration and repatriment agent for the county of Northumberland, where a goodly number of Aeadians are located and a good many more are expected to return from the States and other countries, having left New Bruns-

wick in past years in the hope of bettering their condition.
Three years ago Father Legace founded Legaceville, and today there are a hundred families residing there, and with the help the Department of the Interior is giving them, the movement from the United States and other places to get back on the land will result in the addition, so Mr. Robidoux hopes, of three hundred families during next year.
Speaking of the school question in New Brunswick, Mr. Robidoux, a.flter referring to the troubles some years ago when Mgr. Sweeny was bishop of St. John, stated that the compromise arrived at between the then head of the church in New Brunswick and the Hon. John Boyd, an eminent citizen of [DOT]that city, and a strong friend of the late Sir Leonard Tilley, resulted in making peaoe between the warring factions of that province.
Resolutions in parliament year after year had been unavailing, but goodwill did the work, and although Mr. Robidoux declares that the system is not perfect from a Catholic point of view, he has reason to be pleased with the situation, as it now exists. In virtue of this compromise religious instruction is permitted in the schools under certain conditions. In the Acadian centres the teaching of French prevails, although the compromise made no mention of the fact.
' We have a series of French books,' he added, ' prepared by a commission composed of Father Bourgeois, of St. Joseph's College, Memramoook; Abbe Dagnaud, at one time Superior of St. Ann's College, Nova Scotia, and Mr. Charles Hebert, one of the New Brunswick school inspectors, and others. Thanks to the intelligent co-operation of our friends, we now have a French department at the Normal school in New Brunswick, which is under the direction of Professor Beliveau, of that province also. Under the administration of the Hon. Mr. Hazen, now Minister of Marine and Fisheries, we had adopted by the Council of Public Instruction, a history of Canada, written in French by Father Bourgeois, and destined for the French schools of the province of New Brunswick, which will permit the young Acadian children to learn in their own tongue the history of this country. In several centres, like Moncton, Buetouche, Memramcook, Shediac and elsewhere, nuns who hold provincial licenses to teach in the schools, and although we do not have separate schools in name, we have them in practice. Obligatory instruction i9 discretional according to the will of the ratepayers, and only exists in populous centres, such as St. John, Fredericton and other places, while the price of school books was diminished by half, a year following the advent of the hon. Mr. Hazen to power.
Sir, the hon. member for Kent, N.B., a Canadian of French extraction and a Catholic, has added, whilst speaking to us on the same lines since the beginning of that agitation in Quebec:
Friends of Quebec, we belong to your race and creed; you are the strongest member of the French family on this continent; we certainly need your help and your sympathies, but do not proceed by means of violent Mr. CODERRE.
agitation, have rather recourse to quiet ways and sunny smiles. In the past, according to my own experience, instead of helping us out of our difficulties by agitating, you nave added to those difficulties.
This is and has been my policy:	This
is the policy of my church, as enunciated in an encyclical of the Holy Father, Pope Leo XIII, addressed on the 8th September, 1897, to the archbishops, bishops and other ordinaries of the Dominion of Canada, in relation to the settlement of the Manitoba school question made that year by the right hon. the leader of the opposition of to-day, then Prime Minister of Canada, and the Hon. Mr. Greenway, then Premier of Manitoba. This document can be found in ' Hansard ' of 1898, vol. 2, page 5338:
We are not unaware that something has been done to amend that law. The men who are at the head of the Federal government, and of the province of Manitoba, have already taken certain measures with a view to decreasing the difficulties of which the Catholics of Manitoba complain, and against which they rightly continue to protest. We have no reason to doubt that these measures were taken - from a love of justice and from a laudable motive. We cannot, however dissimulate the truth, the law which they had passed to repair the injury is defective unsuitable, insufficient. The Catholics ask' and no one can deny that they justly ask for much more. Moreover, in the remedial measures that have been proposed there is this defect, that by reason of changed local circumstances they may easily become valueless. In a word, the rights of Catholics and the education of their children have not been sufficiently provided for in Manitoba. Everything in this question demands'-and it is conformable to justice-that they should be thoroughly provided for, that is, by placing in security and surrounding with due safeguards those unchangeable and sacred principles of which we have spoken above. This should be the aim, this the end to be zealously and prudently sought for. Nothing can be more injurious to the attainment of this end than discord. Unity of spirit and harmony of action are most necessary. Nevertheless, since, as frequently happens in things of th's nature, there is not one fixed and determined, but various ways of arriving at the end which is proposed and which should be obtained, it follows that there may be various opinions equally good and advantageous. Therefore, let each and all be mindful of the rules of moderation, gentleness and mutual Charity, let no one fail in the respect that is due to another, but let all resolve in fraternal unanimity, and not without your advice, ito do that which the circumstances require, and which appears best to be done.
In a pastoral of His Grace, the Archbishop of Quebec, of that time, Mgr. Tas-chereau, ' To the clergy and Catholic people of Canada,' commenting upon the abovequoted encyclical, we read, page 5342, of ' Hansard ' of 1898, volume II:

Nothing remains to ns now hut to appeal to that spirit of faith and submission with which we know you to be animated towards the Hoiy See. We are desirous to proclaim it aloud. We are above all political parties. We have no intention to be bound to any. What we desire is the triumph of a sacred cause and not the triumph of a party. And this triumph, we hope that all men of heart, all friends of justice and liberty will help us to obtain it. There is no question of coming back upon an unfortunate fact; this is the hour for a complete, entire reparation that we expect, and that hour, all sympathies, every noible courage, every generous kindness must strive to hasten. Let publio men, therefore, unite together and have recourse to the means that wisdom and patriotism shall inspire them with to put an end to the violent state of things we are all enduring, p. 5343. In the name of justice, in the name of that harmony that should reign among all the citizens of the same country, we invite Protestants-whom this diversity of belief does not prevent from being our brothers-to give us their help and to work with us.
This was also the policy of Mr. Henri Bourassa, then member for Labelle. In a speech he made in relation to the said settlement of the Manitoba School Question.
' Hansard ' of 1898, volume II, page 5437, we find:
I do not want to enter again upon the quarrels of the past. 1 think we have already had too many divisions between the two parties on this question.
Mr. Bourassa at page 5431, says:
I believe firmly that this school question will be settled, and settled on account of the position taken by this government, a position which has been met by the goodwill of the Greenway government, which has given more since this government come into power than during the whole time when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office. I hope this is the last we shall hear of this question, not because we are afraid of it or afraid of the position that we and this government have taken.
All I can add is this: By advocating the policy adhered to in 1897 and since, a policy which commends itself to-day even more than in 1897 to all wise and patriotic men, I sincerely believe I am doing my duty, all my duty, to the Roman Catholic population.
If I err in that respect,-and I do not think I do,-I err in very good company, with men who have never for a moment believed that they acted as traitors in 1896 and after.
Sir, before resuming my chair, though I am still a young member in this House, without much experience, I shall take the liberty of expressing to the right hon. leader of the opposition what I think of his attitude on this question. It is the duty of any member in this House, who does not approve of this Bill, to say so. This duty cannot be deemed to have been
fulfilled by criticising the provisions which the Bill embodies. A Bill may be defective, not only by what it contains, but also by what it does not contain. In this case, some members have protested that the Bill does not embody a clause safeguarding and protecting the rights and principles of the minority in respect to education. When the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) spoke on his amendment, he alluded very vaguely to that question by affirming that a certain agitation was going on in the province of Quebec on account of that omission, but he personally took no stand whatever on that matter; he contented himself by saying that he would wait until some member on this side of the House had given his own view on the point at issue. The right hon. gentleman said, to use his own words, he was waiting within ' the lines of Torres Vedras.' What do we know of Torres Vedras ?
Torres Vedras, a town of Portugal, in the district of Lisbon. Here were the noted fortifications known as the ' lines of Torres Vedras/ constructed by Wellington in 1810, during the Peninsular war.
These elaborate works, history tells us, had been constructed in the course of a year by thousands of Portuguese labourers, directed by Colonel Fletcher, of the Royal Engineers, upon a plan carefu>lly_ thought out and laid down by Wellington himself.
When Massena had oarefully inspected the stupendous barrier reared in front of him, his welldrained eye recognized it as impregnable; he paused for some weeks under semblance of blockading the British forces, while he was really scouring the country for the means of feeding his own; but in November he began to retreat upon Santarem, Almeida and Ciudad Rodrigo, with a half-starved and dis-spirited army, greatly reduced in numbers during the campaign.
I would humbly beg the right hon. gentleman not to desecrate the glorious souvenir which has come to us through those words, ' the lines of Torres Vedras.' Do you believe, Sir, that the brave French general Massena did not know whom he would encounter by attacking this * stupendous barrier.' He knew, Sir, that Wellington and his valiant troops were behind these liues; he knew that those British soldiers had an ideal: the defence of the freedom of the Spanish and Portugese peoples, which freedom the ambitious Napoleon the First was willing to take away from them; he knew that they would fight for that principle till death. And, Sir, that knowledge had much to do towards the decision of Massena to pass by without attacking. There was, Sir, on that ' stupendous barrier,' a glorious flag, the Union Jack, the symbol of liberty the world over, within and without the empire, with one exception, however, as far as the province of Manitoba is concerned: the liberty of

the Roman Catholic population in respect to education.
But what do we see here? The spectacle we have before us does not justify at all the right hon. genleman in comparing his own attitude and the attitude of his party, on this very important question with the attitude of Wellington and his soldiers at Torres Vedras in 1810. That great political party has no policy to offer the House; if these politicians, Sir, have such a policy, they have not the courage to stand openly by it. We see no flag, Sir, flying bravely on top of their lines of battle. I know they have two, though; but their political cunning advises them that those flags should remain in the dark till the day of the election comes. And then, Sir, those who do not know the hon. gentleman will be surprised to find one of those two flags in the province of Quebec, bearing the motto, ' Separate schools for Keewatin,' and the other one flying in the other province-with in its folds the slogan, ' Hands off Manitoba.'
Sir, if there were lions within the lines of Torres Vedras, there are political foxes on those opposition seats. These tactics have succeeded once in 1896; but I really believe that this country will not consent to be deceived once more.
Sir, I really hope that this message of good-will, of harmony and of concord, that we, on this side of the House, are just sending to the people of Manitoba, will bring them to give, in their plenitude, to my Roman Catholic compatriots in Manitoba the rights and privileges in respect to education which a judgment of the highest tribunal of the empire in the Brophy case has decided that they were entitled to. Knowing the past of the Conservative partv in Manitoba, that the Hon, Mr. Roblin had been defending, against Greenway, Martin and Sifton, the separate schools attacked by the law of 1890, that he was by the side of Sir Charles Tup-per in 1896 to obtain that the rights and privileges of the minority, as embodied in a remedial law, presented in compliance with the judgment rendered in the Brophy case, and which gave complete satisfaction to the interested parties, should become the law of the province of Manitoba;-knowing moreover^ that since he has obtained power -and, Sir, history will tell us that the Conservatives could not get into power in Manitoba, only after the great agitation raised by the_ Liberals against them on that school question had cooled down-he did all that he could to alleviate the harm the law of 1890 and its amendment have done to the cause of the Roman Catholics of Manitoba, I really believe that the Hon. Mr. Roblin, whose already very high reputation as a statesman will be greatly increased by this success of his policy, will take advantage of the feelings of joy and Mr. CODEREE.
enthusiasm brought to his own people by the passing of this measure, to at last give fair justice to my compatriots of Manitoba. Sir, I have the greatest and sincerest admiration and love for the British flag. It is on account of that admiration and that love that I most deeply desire that that dark spot put on that flag by the Liberal Chieftain Greenway in 1890 would at last disappear. We are told tnat the Hon. Mr. Roblin has had the very patriotic idea to order that the Union Jack should fly over and above each and every public school in Manitoba. It will be a day of universal contentment and joy, all over the land, when the Roman Catholic children, frequenting these schools, will feel that that great flag shelters and protects all their rights, privileges and liberty, and that they are on a footing of equality with their young comrades of other extraction. Sir, thanks to the policy of the present government, I feel that we will soon see that day.
I feel confident, Sir, that taking the course I am taking, I have done my duty, not only to the Roman Catholic population of Manitoba and Keewatin, but to the whole population of our country.

Mr. Speaker, much as I believe that the province of Manitoba is entitled to the extension of boundaries which it is to receive under the Bill which we are now considering, I have felt it my duty to oppose the passage of this Bill for reasons which I have already stated to the House, and1 which were set forth in the amendment which I proposed, namely, that the terms granted to Manitoba were at once unfair to that province and to the rest of the Dominion as well. My right hon. friend opposite, speaking some time afterwards, characterized that amendment as a piece of political strategy to avoid an impending political difficulty in connection with this Bill. Let me say to my right hon. friend that if I thought it advisable in this matter to resort to political strategy, I would1 think it best to play the game as well as I could. But there. are occasions when it is not advisable to resort to political strategy, when me question before the House has to be squarely met, and this is. the position I intend to take now. There are two considerations which, for me, dominate the present situation, Manitoba is entitled to an extension of its boundaries, not only for the welfare of Manitoba itself, but for the welfare of' the whole Dominion. The territory which it is now proposed to give to Manitoba has been, up to the present time, a sealed book as far as the white man is concerned. The white man has never penetrated into tfhik territory except as a hunter. He is now going in as a permanent settler. A railway is actually in course of construction from

the wheat fields of the western provinces to the waters of Hudson bay, and, therefore, it follows as a necessity that this territory must be given provincial organization. Municipal institutions have to be established, civil institutions have to be established likewise, towns will grow, and all the other accompaniments of civilized life will have to be attended to. Therefore, as a matter of necessity, this territory must be either organized as a province or annexed to another province. Nobody can contend that it would be advisable, opportune, or politic, for reasons well known to everybody, that a new province should be constituted out of that territory. It must be annexed to another province, and1 the only province to which it can be annexed is the province of Manitoba. Then, Manitoba, from the fact of this annexation, is entitled to receive, for the purpose of revenue, either the lands of the territory or an equivalent in money. Beyond this, everything that is contained in this Bill, and there is much contained in it, is in violation of the Tights of the other provinces.
Hear, hear.

Manitoba has been for forty years in this Dominion. It has been on a footing of equality, in so far as provincial subsidies are concerned, with the other provinces, and now you take it from that condition of equality and give it favoured treatment. It seems to me that my hon. friend opposite has not measured the length to which this concession is going to lead him. He has raised problems which, evidently, he never dreamed of in his philosophy. But already, from all sides, troubles have arisen for him and for the country. I can say fairly that the troubles which will face him do not disturb me very much-that is his own con-cern

But I cannot be indifferent to the condition of the country; and it does seem to me manifest that the other provinces will not be satisfied unless there is a reorganization of the whole of the provincial subsidies which we thought we had secured for all time in the amendment to the constitution, which was passed by the Imperial parliament in 1907. Now, whilst Manitoba is given extravagant terms, for which there can 'be no justification whatever, on the other hand that province is treated in a manner which cannot be defended by any man who values the rights of the province. Manitoba had the right to expect from the men who form the present government, when they were in opposition, that she would receive her lands, but instead of her being given her lands, a portion of her lands have been given to another province. Here again the government is introducing a new principle which is
fraught with dire consequences. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, stated some days ago in this debate, that if Manitoba was not given the extension of her territory during the regime of the preceding administration, it was because I wanted to penalize that province the government of which was not composed of friends of my own.
Hear, hear.

Nobody at this moment, or indeed at any moment, can quote a word or a syllable of mine which could justify such an imputation. I would like to ask anybody who has seen me in opposition or in office for more than thirty years in this House, if any imputation of that kind could be based on anything I ever said or anything I ever did. Sir, it is useless to refute such a statement as that. When Manitoba came to ask for the extension of her boundaries, I thought it advisable before considering her application, that her neighbour to the east and her neighbour to the west should be consulted. Can anybody in this Hause say that it was not the first of all things to be done? I had a conference summoned, composed of members representing Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Ontario. Manitoba was not represented by friends of mine, Ontario was not represented by friends of mine, but Saskatchewan was represented by friends of mine. Saskatchewan made application there and then for the territory which is now given to Manitoba, and I said tb my friend from Saskatchewan, Mr. Walter Scott, the premier of the province, that in my humble judgment, ,in all fairness and equity that territory should go to Manitoba, and I reported accordingly to my colleagues, and to the House. * Now the province of Saskatchewan is coming forward with a new request. It is asking that since it could not have ihe territory, it should have access to the waters of Hudson bay in the same manner that Ontario has access to that bay. If, Sir, it is right to give to Ontario 800,000 acres, or thereabouts of the lands of Manitoba, together with access to Hudson bay, is there any reason in the world, why the same measure of treatment should not be given to Saskatchewan as well?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the right hon. gentleman, but with reference to a Bill which was before the House last night motions were made to refer it back to the Committee of the Whole, and I was obliged to rule that those who were speaking should confine themselves to the amendments that were proposed to the Bill, as I regarded that to be the proper ruling of the Chair. To-night the amendment has been moved that this Bill be

referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions that they have power to amend the measure by inserting a clause in reference to the educational rights of the minority. Following the same rule, I would be obliged, of course, to decide that the right hon. gentleman is not speaking strifctly to !the question. But if it is the desire of the House that the debate should be of an unrestricted character, covering the whole scope of the Bill, I certainly have no objection; but I do not wish it to be understood that I desire to rule one way one night and rule to give a reverse ruling another.

I would bow most respectfully to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and I am all the more grateful to you since I was not in order that you did not interrupt me sooner because I have about finished what I have to say on that particular point. I might perhaps be allowed, without trespassing on the time of the House, and on your ruling, Sir, to finish what I intended to say. In my humble judgment Saskatchewan had as much claim as Ontario to the same treatment, and with that statement I will close this part of my argument. I now come, Sir, to another matter, the matter which is involved in the amendment that is now before the House. My young and hon. friend who has just addressed the House and also the hon. member from Vercheres (Mr. Rainville), I understand, though I was not here at the time, commented somewhat adversely upon the fact that I had stated at a former stage of the debate that I was within the lines of Torres Vedras.
Hear, hear.

If I was
within the lines of Torres Vedras it was not with any intention of remaining there permanently. My hon. friend who has just addressed the House stated that the Duke of Wellington was within the lines of Torres Vedras. That is true, but as everybody knows the Duke of Wellington came out from the lines of Torres Vedras, and came out with some effect upon the army of the enemy. If I have taken that position, Sir, it was with no intention whatever of shirking an expression of my opinion, in which I am very proud to see hon. gentlemen on the other side seem to take some interest, but it was because I did not think that it was advisable for me to enter so early in the debate when so far, the debate was not within the two sides of the House, but altogether within the government side of the House.
If the question has been brought before the House-this family question-in con-Mr. SPEAKER.
nection with the boundaries of Manitoba, the debate was not raised from this side but from the other side of the House. I think it would have been rather imprudent in me to interfere in that family quarrel. I think it was my part to keep out of it and see what position was taken by hon. gentlemen opposite. I have a word to say to hon. gentlemen on the other side. But before I proceed further, I must say that, for my part, I approach this question at the moment, not in my capacity as leader of a party, but as an individual, I do not want to bind anybody to my own opinion on a question of this kind; I leave it to the judgment and conscience of every one of those who have honoured me in the past, or to-day honour me, with their confidence. But I never meant anybody to be in doubt as to what my attitude would be on this question. My attitude upon this question is well known; it has been well known for the last sixteen years. I stand, in this year 1912 on the same platform on which I stood in 1896. I would not then interfere with the autonomy of Manitoba; I will not now when in opposition interfere with the autonomy of Manitoba.
As regards this amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Yamaska (Mr. Mon-dou), to my mind, it is beyond doubt, and I think ought to be beyond doubt to himself, that if his object was to maintain in the new territory of Manitoba the legislation upon which he has based his amendment, the legislation of 1875, he could not have taken-I hope he will allow me to say so without offense-a more ineffective way of doing it. I think it has been demonstrated to him that the amendment which he has proposed even if it had been adopted by this House, would not in any way add to the rights or privileges of the minority in the new territory accorded1 to them in the Manitoba Act. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), has argued, and my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), also has argued, that this whole question is a question of law. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has been particularly emphatic upon that point, This is indeed a question of law, and, so far as this amendment is concerned, it is nothing but a question of law. But, though this is a question of law, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, who comes from the province of Quebec, is well aware that it is as a political question that we must look at it at this moment. My hon. friend is well aware that for the last fifteen years it has been stated by all the forces of the party to which he belongs in that province that the settlement we made of the actual question in 1896, was no settlement at all, and that if the party to which he belongs were returned to office, the first thing they

would do would be to tear that settlement to pieces and restore to the minority in Manitoba the full system of separate schools they had prior to 1890. That is the battle we have had to fight at every election since 1896. In 1900, in 1904, in 1908, the same question was always discussed. It was declared that I, in particular, as leader of the party then in office, had betrayed my fellow-religionists, that the settlement we had made was in violation of the clear injunction of the Privy Council, that we were in default, that the settlement was invalid, and that as soon as the Conservative administration was returned to office, all this would be set aside, and' the minority in Manitoba would be put back into the position they held in 1890. Everybody within the sound of my voice who comes from the province of Quebec knows that I am not in any way exaggerating the case, but that I have stated it as it was stated over and over again by the party to which my hon. friend belongs, in every election we have had since 1896.
Let us look at this question. I agree with something that was said by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice this afternoon. We are a people of many origins and man.y creeds; but there is no class in this country which, by reason of creed, race or any other consideration, can claim to have rights indefeasible and superior to the rights of any other class. All the classes have Tights, and all these rights are limited by the rights of the other classes. And whenever there is a clash of interests, as unfortunately there have been too many in the past, it behooves the minority to be moderate in its claims, it behooves the majority to be generous in its treatment of the minoritv. But, if any class in this community insists upon its pound of flesh according as it may be written in the bond, and if all the other classes meet such pretensions in a similar manner, the result must be a condition of affairs not far removed from anarchy. The policy I have advocated ever since I have entered public life, the policy upon which I fought the elections of 1896, is that all such clashing of interests, whenever and wherever they occur, must be settled and can be settled only through compromise, through conciliation, and through anneal to all interested parties to make some sacrifices of opinion, and even pretensions, yes, and even of rights, in order to come to an understanding of peace, wood-will and harmony in this land. I was elected on that platform, and upon that platform I stood so long as I was in office, not only upon this question of education, which came to the front on more than one occasion, during the term of office of the late administration, but even on all similar matters in which their was a clashing of interests. May I recall to the recollection of the House, for
instance, our method of dealing with the problem which has been agitating the province of British Columbia for many years, the problem of Asiatic .immigration.
There is in British Columbia constant cause of trouble arising out of Asiatic immigration. This is not due to any prejudice of colour, this is not due to any ill-will, but it is the result of economic conditions which prevail in British Columbia. It has been shown that whenever ' Asiatic labour ' comes into competition in the labour market with white labour, there is an immediate cause of disturbance. The reason is obvious, it is that the standard of Oriental civilization as compared with our own civilization is very different, and the Asiatic labourer is able, on a lower wage than the white man, to live in comparative comfort, whereas it is not possible for a white man to accept such a wage. The consequence is that we had in British Columbia a constant source of trouble. When we came into office in 1896 we were approached by a majority of the members of the government of British Columbia, who were then in sympathy with the government, with [DOT] a request to increase the capitalization tax upon Chinese immigrants which had been put on the statute-book by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1885, and to which we had no objection. We were asked at the same time to impose a similar tax upon the subjects of His Majesty the Japanese Emperor. To that we would not agree, and why? Why did we think it advisable to put a capitation tax upon Chinamen and not upon Japanese? The reason was that there had been recently signed between the King of England and the Emperor of Japan a treaty of alliance, to a large extent offensive and defensive, and it would have been an indignity to put such a stigma upon the subjects of our ally. So, instead of putting that indignity upon the subjects of the Emperor of Japan, we sent to Japan one of our colleagues, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) to settle that question; and by pursuing a policy of conciliation between the two countries we were able to obtain from the Japanese Emperor an engament that he himself would restrict Japanese immigration within a certain limit, and the result has been that since then we have had peace in British Columbia. True it is that the course then followed was not satisfactory to the people of British Columbia; but I believe that I am within the judgment of the House in saying that the policy was not only a strong one, but was eminently wise.
In the same manner we settled the school question that had been a source of trouble in Manitoba previous to 1896; in the same manner we settled the school question in

Saskatchewan and Alberta by the Autonomy Bills of 1905. Ail these questions, burning as they were, we settled by a policy of compromise, of conciliation, by an appeal to the good sense, and better judgment, and better heart of all the parties interested. But Sir, that policy of conciliation and of compromise was denounced with the greatest possible severity in the province of Quebec, by all the forces of the Conservative party, and by none with greater bitterness and severity than the hon. gentlemen whom I now see before me on the treasury benches, my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) and my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel). These hon. gentlemen and their friends, in the press and on the platform, denounced compromise as humiliating, denounced conciliation as weak, and this they preached in season and out of season, in public prints, in the press, and everywhere they could get a hearing. Wherever they could find a stump for their two feet they preached the policy of no concession. Their plea was:	We want the plentitude of the
rights of the minority in the province of Manitoba restored to them, and if the Conservative party is returned to power we will give them tlhat plenitude of rights. Now Sir, am I exaggerating? Everybody knows that this has been the policy of hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House. Everybody knows that they have maintained that policy from 1895-6 up to the 5th of March. 1912, when, within our hearing, and to the dismay of their followers, they declared that the settlement which was made in 1897, whether good or bad, was binding, and that there was nothing more to be done for the minority in the province of Manitoba. Sir, there is no doubt whatever that if the speeches that we heard on the 5th of March, a week ago, to-morrow, from the mouth of the Minister of Public Works, and from the mouth of the Postmaster General, had been heard during the last election in the province of Quebec, the result would have been somewhat different from what it was. The general result would have been different, as to the individual result, I daresay the Minister of Public Works might have squeezed into his seat by the skin of his teeth, but even of that I am not very sure. But as to my hon. friend the Postmaster General, he would never have come within 1,000 votes of obtaining the seat of the county of Quebec.
Heaven, Sir, is my witness, that so far as I am personally concerned, the defeat of the 21st September last never caused me a moment of pain, I certainly regretted it for the party, and I still more regretted it for the country. But I repeat, that it: Sir WILFRID LAURIER,
never affected me personally in the least. I do not know but that I am rather glad than otherwise, for this reason, that the defeat of the Liberal party gives us the measure of the men who have replaced us, and the people of Quebec will understand now that all these loud professions and promises of restoring the rights of the minority in Manitoba were simply snares and shams made to reach office, and to be disavowed as soon as office was reached. The people of Quebec will now understand that I and my friends did not deceive them when we told them that the school question had been settled in 1897, and that these gentlemen who boasted that they would re-open it, never could re-open it at all, because it was settled for all time. The country has gained this much, that we shall have no more agitation upon this subject; the country has gained this much, that we shall know where we are, and that forever this question is removed from the field of agitation.
My hon. friend the Postmaster General and my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, in order to cover their retreat, went very far back upon the record and threshed the old straw over and over again threshed before. They said, in order to cover their retreat, that the settlement which I made with the government of Manitoba of the school question in 1897, had gone behind the judgment of the Privy Council, and had been at variance with its dispositions. I have to take issue with my hon. friends upon that point. I say that the settlement which we made in 1897 in no way contravened the dispositions of the judgment of the Privy Council. I say that the Privy Council never ordered the restoration of separate schools in Manitoba.
I say more; I say that the minority in Manitoba, before the Privy Council, never asked for a complete restoration of separate schools as they existed before 1890. This is a broad statement on my part. I say that the minority in Manitoba, before the Privy Council, never asked for the full restoration of the school system which existed nrior to the legislation of 1890. For what I say now I will give book and verse. I will quote from the argument of the counsel of the minority, Mr. Ewart. This is the thoughtful argument with which he summed up the case. I beg hon. gentlemen to give me their attention while I read the argument presented then by Mr. Ewart as to what were the conditions of the minority in Manitoba. This is the language that was used by Mr. Ewart:
Before closing I would like to say a word or two as to what we are seeking. As it has been already remarked, we are not asking for any declaration as to the extent of the relief to be given by the Governor General. We

merely ask that it should be held that he has jurisdiction to hear our prayer, and to grant us some relief if he thinks proper to do so. It may be that the Dominion authorities may not choose to re-establish us in all the rights and privileges which we enjoyed prior to this Act of 1890, although that was acquiesced in by everybody, and it remained as a good working Act for a period of nineteen years, and although I may say also that that is the system, or almost the system, which has existed in the province of Quebec for more than a quarter of a century, it may be that the Dominion authorities may prefer the Ontario system, under which there is a closer governmental control-a system under which government control is very complete, under which books are chosen by the government inspectors appointed by government, and all school regulations are made by government. Or it may he that some other system may be devised which will enable the Roman Catholics to teach in schools to which no Protestant child now goes, the religion of its parents under limited circumstances, without thereby being penalized by ostracism from the public school provisions. We cannot tell, nor have I come here instructed to state what the measure of relief will he which will be asked if it be held that the Governor General has jurisdiction to deal with this matter, hut this much I think I may properly say that we have no desire to withdraw from the operation of state statutory control. That position we never did possess under the Manitoba statutes, and we do not see-nor, indeed, can we ask-to be placed in any better position than the position which we occupied prior to the Act of 1890.
Is there in these words of the counsel of the minority any statement that they asked for the fall restoration of the system which was abolished in 1890? They simply asked that it be decided that the Governor in Council had the right to hear their request, that he had power to interfere, leaving it to the Governor in Council to provide such relief as he might think proper after having looked into the circumstances. That judgment, so clear in itself, has been represented for fifteen years by the gentlemen who now sit on the treasury benches as an order from the Privy Council to the government of Canada, to the government of Manitoba and to every person else concerned, to restore Catholic schools as they existed prior to 1890. All they asked was in the very words of counsel, some relief, leaving it to the discretion of the government according to the circumstances, to give it in larger or smaller measure, as it might be decided. This is the order which was made by the lords of the Privy Council. I would also_ ask the indulgence of the House if I cite at some length from the judgment of the Privy Council. Their lordships say:
As a matter of fact the objection of Roman Catholics to schools such as alone receive state
aid under the Act of 1890 is conscientious and deeply rooted. If this had not been so, if there had been a system of public education acceptable to Catholics and Protestants alike, the elaborate enactments which have been the subject of so much controversy and consideration would have been unnecessary.
And then it goes on to the concluding part:
For the reasons which have been given, their lordships are of opinion that the 2nd subsection of section 22 of ' The Manitoba Act' is the governing enactment and that appeal to the Governor General in Council was admissible by virtue of that enactment, on the grounds set forth in the memorials and petitions, inasmuch as the Acts of 1890 affected rights and privileges of the Roman Catholic minority in relation to education within the meaning of that subsection. The further question is submitted whether the Governor in Council has power to make the declarations or remedial orders asked for in the memorials or petitions or has any other jurisdiction in the premises. Their lordships have decided that the Governor General in Council has jurisdiction and that the appeal is well founded, but the particular course to he pursued must be determined by the authorities to whom it has been committed by the statute. It is not for this tribunal to intimate the precise steps to he taken. Their general character is sufficiently defined by the 3rd subsection of section 22 of ' The Manitoba Act.
It is certainly not essential that the statutes repealed by the Act of 1890 should be re-enacted or that the preoise provisions of these statutes should again be made law. The system of education embodied in the Acts of 1890 no doubt commends itself to and adequately supplies the wants of the great majority of the inhabitants of the province. All legitimate ground of complaint would be removed if that system were supplemented by provisions which would remove the grievance upon which the appeal is founded and wer.e modified as far as might he necessary to give effect to these provisions.
Mark my words. No order here to restore the Catholic schools as they existed previous to 1890! Their lordships on the contrary are clear to state that there would be no necessity of repealing the Act of 1890 which was satisfactory to the majority but in order to remove the grievance of the minority they suggested that it should be supplemented by some such legislation or some such mode as would allow them to bring up their children in their own faith in so far as the schools were concerned. Upon this there was a remedial order issued, an (order which, was issued certainly very imprudently, without sufficient information, without taking into consideration what clashing of interests there might be in Manitoba and that order simply instructed the province of Manitoba to restore effectively and actually the system of separate schools

which had been in existence prior to 1890. Three things are necessary to constitute separate schools; first of all separate organization; second, exemption from taxation for public schools, and in the third place an adequate share of the provincial funds allotted to education.
These things were ordered in the Remedial Order of the previous government. The government of Manitoba was ordered to enact a law which would give back to the minority
(a) The right to build, maintain, equip, manage conduct and support Roman Catholic schools in the manner provided by the said statutes which were repealed by the two Acts of 1890 aforesaid.
(h) The right to share proportionately in any grant made out of the public funds for the purposes of education.
(c) The right of exemption of such Roman Catholics as contribute to Roman Catholic schools from all payment or contribution to the support of any other schools.
The great mistake which was made by the government of Sir Mackenzie Bowell in that Remedial Order was that they were ordering the province of Manitboa to do more than they who had passed the Order could enforce. If the province of Manitoba refused to comply with the Order, they could very well have passed a Bill which would exempt the minority from paying taxes to the public schools, they could very well have passed an Act giving the right to the minority to organize their own schools, but they could not by any Act of legislation or by order in council, or in any manner whatever, give away the funds of the province of Manitoba to the separate schools. And in this they made a fatal mistake; they introduced a Bill and, just as we had anticipated, while the Bill authorized the legislature to pass a Separate School Act, to exempt from taxation the supporters of separate schools, they could not give to the schools any share in the public moneys and therefore, if the Remedial Bill had become law, the schools which might have b'een organized could not have received any funds out of the public treasury; they would have been at once placed in a position of inferiority and therefore the settlement could not be satisfactory to the minority.
We came into office upon that issue. We made a settlement with the province of Manitoba. I do not pretend that the settlement we made with Manitoba was perfect, but I affirm it was the best thing that could be done for the minority in Manitoba; I never pretended that it was, but I say, without any hesitation, that it was far better than the provisions which were made in the Remedial Bill. It was as^ good as coulld be obtained under existing circumstances, after this Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
question had been for six years the battleground of factions in Manitoba. My hon. friend the Postmaster Genera], in his speech the other day, said that the settlement which had been made had not been efficient. I take complete issue with him upon that point, and I think I might call witnesses to this, but it will be sufficient if I state here what the settlement was and how it was worked. The settlement that we made with the government of Mr. Greenw.ay at that time was that wheTe-ever in any school in a town or city there was an average attendance of 40 children of the Roman Catholic faith, they would have a right to have a teacher of their own persuasion. In rural districts where there was an average attendance of 25 children, they would have the right to obtain from the trustees a teacher of their own persuasion, and a right, at certain times and under certain conditions to be determined by the trustees, to have religious education in the schools. Children speaking the French language would have the right to receive their instruction in French. That was the' tenor of the settlement we made with Manitoba.
My hon. friend tells me, and told tile House the other day, that that settlement was inefficient. I tell him, and I think I will not be contradicted by anybody here, that that agreement has been put into operation in at least 200 schools in the province of Manitoba, and1 it has given complete satisfaction. The only places in which it has not given any satisfaction are Brandon and Winnipeg, and the reason for that, as I understand, and I speak subject to correction, is that the settlement was not put in operation in These cities. For reasons which I do not know, or rather which I know too well, this settlement was not put in operation in those cities, but everywhere else it was put in operation, and I repeat that wherever it has been put in operation outside of these two cities it has given fairly general satisfaction. That is the position to-day, that is the position which was denounced in the province of Quebec for no other reason that I can see except the desire of obtaining power at all costs.
I now come to the question oi the existing condition of things in the territory to be annexed und'er this Bill to Manitoba. There is no doubt whatever that the law of 1875 is in operation to-day in those territories, and were that territory organized to-day, as was stated by the Minister of Justice this afternoon, the minority would have the right to all its provisions. But that is not a constitutional right, it is simply a legislative enactment of this parliament under the control of this parliament so long as that territory remains

under its jurisdiction, but no further than that. If this were a constitutional agreement or right, there would be no necessity to put it in any law, because it would carry itself as a constitutional right wherever the territories might be placed. But there is this objection. The young members who have followed their leaders so far now believe that the grievances of Manitoba would be relieved as they want them to be relieved. There is this objection to the incorporation of the law of 1875 in the present Bill, which would give full separate school rights to that part of the country, that such an enactment would not be worth the paper on which it was printed because we cannot impose it on Manitoba. Unless Manitoba agrees to this law this parliament has no authority to. force it upon Manitoba. This would have been a case for compromise, a case for conciliation, but my non. friends who sit on the treasury benches from the province of Quebec despise conciliation, and have contempt for compromise. Their policy was everything or nothing, and' the result is nothing.
My hon. friend, the Postmaster General, the other day stated three or four times that he was fully assured1 that Mr. Eoblin was well disposed towards the minority, that he was disposed to give to the minority as much as or more than was given in the law of 1875. If, Sir, Mr. Eoblin is so well disposed, it would have been an excellent occasion to make the compromise or settlement proposed. Indeed there might have been no necessity for a compromise.
If Mr. Eoblin is so well disposed, perhaps he v/ould have given everything on the asking. My hon. friend told us with great positiveness that he was assured of the disposition of Mr Eoblin. We could not understand where his assurance came from, because he told us that he had no understanding with Mr. Eoblin. But he was sure of his facts. How did lie know5 Was it a case of telepathy, or did a little bird come from Winnipeg and whisper in his ear that, it would be all right? I have to point out to my hon. friend that if the law of 1875, giving the full right to separate schools to the minority, has not been incorporated in this Bill, it is because there are men beside him and men behind him who would not have this disposition incorporated in this Bill. I have no doubt that my hon. friend the Postmaster General, and also my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, made a pretty ardent request to their colleagues to save them from the humiliating position in which they would be placed, if the school rights were not restored to the minority. At least, I give them that credit. I suppose my hon. friend the Postmaster General, made the request to his colleagues, not from the love he may bear to the min156
ority, but for the good name he wants to give to the Postmaster General. But he could not obtain his request. Mr. Eoblin, I am prepared to believe, is well disposed, but Mr. Eoblin has some men behind him also, who may not allow that fair disposition to materialize, as my hon. friend expects it to materialize. Sir, the public opinion which in 1890 forced the legislature of Manitoba to remove the separate schools as they existed then, was the result of conflicts and passions which I have reason to believe are now passed away. But, Sir, as it happens, very often, those passions have left behind them an aftermath which has not yet passed away, which has still a good deal of force and potentiality. It is with the human race as it is with the elements. When the elements are thrown out of gear by some cataclysm, it takes a long time before they are restored to their normal condition. When the storms have been raging on the ocean, when the waves have been roused to fury, if all of a sudden the winds ceased to blow, the clouds vanish from the horizon, and the sun shines again warm and bright. But though peace now reigns above, peace is not yet restored to the waters below. For a long time the billows continue to be tossed by the internal fury imparted to them by the storm. Though the storm itself has abated, it is a long time before the serenity of the heavens is reflected on the placid bosom of the deep.
Sir, we know only too well from the teaching of history, and from our own experience in this new country, that the passions which rage in the human heart far exceed the violence of winds and waves and storms. We know from our own experience, as well as from the experience of other countries, and from the whole teaching of history, that when in any community popular passions have been driven to wrath, even though the causes of their anger may be removed, still for a long time the community continues to be torn by their violence, and it is only by slow degrees, by mutual forbearance, that peace and harmony again recover their blessed sway. It is in the light of this experience that I have endeavoured to guide the destinies of the party to which I belong since that party entrusted me with its fortunes. I have learned from history, especially from the history of this country, that the best method of vindicating even the most sacred causes, is by moderation and the respect of others as well as the respect of ourselves. I have learned to apply this doctrine even to the settlement of the school question of Manitoba. On that occasion I appealed to the best elements of all parties, of all creeds, of all races, and I think I have succeeded fairly well except with one class the class now sitting on



the treasury benches. Whatever njay have been the reward of my efforts in that direction, the policy which I maintained in office I shall maintain in opposition. Never shall I raise my hand in any way so that discord shall come in this land, and for these considerations I shall vote against the amendment.
