speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to detain the House at this late hour; and indeed, it seemed to me, after the full expression of my views which I gave the other day, that I would not be called upon to speak again on this subject. But, Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow the statement of my right hon. friend this evening to go unchallenged. I knew, when my right hon. friend stated the other day, with studied caution, that he had retired within the lines of Torres Vedras, that he would be chased out of those lines. I must confess that I was somewhat curious to see how he would manoeuvre. I did not for a single moment doubt that he would not, as the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Coderre) has so eloquently portrayed, follow the example of the noble duke whose name is associated with Torres Vedras, but that his issuing from those lines would be coupled with a great deal of gliding and sliding. My right hon. friend, he will pardon me for saying, is getting old; we are all getting old; and he has acquired the habit of self-laudation coupled with the laudation of past times. For quite a while I have noticed that my right hon. friend, with whom my relations have always been most cordial, 'has been given to self-laudation. He is a ' laudator temporis aeti.' He has been singularly faithful to that motto. But ' pride goeth before destruction and haughty snirit before a fall,' and he has fallen into the pit this even ire.
I remember that my rjght hon. friend boasted from his place in the House that he would have a transcontinental line that would1 cost some $13,000,000 or $15,000,000, and that

Order, order.
Mr. MONK-he said it would be paid out of the surplus of one year. We know what came of that assertion.
Order, order.

That was one of those occasions. Another occasion arose when my right hon. friend, at the time which he referred to a moment ago, when we were discussing the Autonomy Bills, said that he stood upon the rock of the constitution, and invited us to come up there with him. Some one on this side of the House beckoned to him, and with the alacrity of a panther he jumped down from the rock, and he bears us illwill because we would Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
not follow him upon that occasion. Let me point out to my right i\on. friend that he has either not followed my humble arid modest career during the past 15 years, or else I must accuse him of having intentionally deceived both the House and the country upon the real attitude which I, and those around me, from 1896 took upon this very question which we are discussing this evening. A few days ago I mentioned in this very debate that before the settlement -in which my right hon. friend appears to be so proud, but to which I will refer in a moment-where he sacrificed shamelessly the rights of those he was bound to protect, I declared that with respect to remedial legislation, the verdict of the people in 1896 was conclusive, that that mode of remedying the grievances of the minority in Manitoba was vetoed by the people. And1 when my right hon. friend, without even consulting the complainants-the minority interested-concluded with the government of Manitoba, which had deprived them of their rights, and alone and ex parte made that settlement; when he brought down Mr. Greenway to Montreal, gave him a triumph, tendered him a banquet, and invited1 all his friends to celebrate that settlement; when we knew the terms of that settlement; when my right hon. friend brought it down and laid it on the table of the House, but was so much ashamed of himself that he failed to put upon the agreement his signature, and that of the man who had concluded it with him-I found, Sir, that that agreement was not a fair one, and that after all his boasts, after all his representations, after all his conciliation, he had finally sacrificed the very people whom it was his duty to protect. That was what we found', that was what I declared, and on no occasion since 1897 have I discussed that question in our province. I have never discussed it, never raised it, never made it an issue
Oh, oh.
What about yourself?

I have no apology to make for myself. Now, in closing, I wish to say this: My right hon. friend has imagined a picture, in comical vein, of my colleagues from the province of Quebec and myself as endeavouring to obtain, by entreaty and prayer and persuasion, from our colleagues in the government, the introduction of some guarantee clause in this Bill. Well, that may have been the mode of proceeding at the time when my right hon. friend was the leader of the government; we have not that habit as yet. I know that there has been-I myself have been the object of considerable obloquy in reference to our position in this matter. It has not put me in a resigning mood.
Oh, oh.

I am very glad to keep the House in good humour. I must say that to me it is absolutely inconceivable-and I think the same remark no doubt applies to my colleagues from the province of Quebec who are very much in the same position as myself-it is absolutely inconceivable, I say, that a man who has the cares and labours and responsibility of the office which I have the honour to hold, should have, past a certain age, any real desire to keep that office if he could decently get out of it. But the obloquy to which I have referred, has not, as I have said, brought me into a resigning mood. On the contrary, I must say that I feel riveted, bolted and barred to the ofiice more than ever before. I should have to

borrow from the language that I learned at my good mother's knee, expressions strong enough to convey how little these insults and invectives have led me in the direction of resignation.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) went deeply into the legal question this afternoon. I cannot claim to have his competency, but I may say that I have looked as deeply as time allowed into what has been called, and is still called among certain people, the vested rights existing in these territories. I find none,-could not find any of any kind. There was a restriction placed upon an administrative officer in case he was surrounded by a clause, in case he was authorized to legislate. He never had the clause without which he could not legislate; he never was authorized to legislate; he never did legislate. The non-Catholics of Quebec have nothing to fear for themselves, in case Manitoba should maintain its stand in favour of public schools, for to apeak of reprisals on the part of the majority is absurd.
We are requested from every quarter to protect the rights of the minority in connection with the annexation of the territory of Keewatin. We are told that we should not follow in the footsteps of the traitors and wretches who did away with these rights in 1896 and 1905. It is all very well to -lay down principles; it is al'l very well to vindicate these courageously, vigorously, and better still to reap encomiums after falling on the battlefield, in the midst of the fray. But to distinguish one's self by such brilliant achievements, by such heroic deeds which lead to immortality, one must at least have the hope that they will ensure some practical result which will be of

actual advantage if not to the hero who sacrifices himself, at any rate to those who will come afterwards. Leonidas defending with his stalwarts the Thermop.ylae knew that he was courting certain death; but his country would be delivered thereby. Salaberry a.nd his men at Chateauguay were fighting under great disadvantages, and might well have been crushed by a much larger force, however, they retained some hope of winning the day. Cambronne at Waterloo answered back to the general who called on him to surrender, those historic words which are characteristic of that chivalrous French race of old, whose spirit still animates us, we the proud descendants of that gallant stock: ' Guardsmen may die, but surrender never.' Why should the French guardsmen who occupy seats in this House, why should that small phalanx of twenty Canadians be expected to accomplish what another French Canadian, with the support of fifty others, refused to do when the time had come to play the hero, and make sacrifices, and assert existing rights which had been confirmed by the highest court in the empire? Why should we be expected to do what a great Canadian supported by fifty others refused to do in 1905, while fortune was smiling upon him, and glory followed his flag and made the earth quake wherever it passed? Why should we be called upon to make such a sacrifice, when for fifteen consecutive years in the province of Quebec there has been a continuous round of applause for the great hero who was digging the grave wherein were buried all our fellow countrymen's rights to separate schools, and to the use of that French language which we learnt on our mother's lap and which has produced the finest literature known to the world?
Why should we be expected to protect rights which legal authorities declare to be non-existent, and which in any case are not interfered with by this Bill of they do exist?
In 1890, while Laurier was working hand in hand with McCarthy and other fanatics cf the same stripe, on this side of the House the Tuppers, the Northrups, the Hazens, the Fosters, the Haggarts and many others were defending the rights which it was still time to defend and safeguard.
But no, the French race will survive in spite of its oppressors; it has successfully pulled through the disasters of 1760 and the persecutions which have been its lot in the meantime, and the miserable dealings of Greenway will come to an end.
In 1896, I had faith in Laurier, a French Canadian and Catholic; I was confident at any rate that he would support by his vote and his eloquence the rights defended even by Protestants.
But no, his mongrel alliance with the twenty-four fanatics who still formed part of the conservative party, resulted in miserable obstructive tactics which prevented sanction being given to the remedial Bill, in spite of a message from His Grace Archbishop Langevin which read as follows: Bill workable, effective and satisfactory; I approve of it. All bishops and true Catholics should do the same. It means salvation. (Signed) Archbishop Langevin.
I shall now quote the following from the letter written by Rev. Father Lacomhe to Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
At this critioal period in connection with the Manitoba school question, allow an aged missionary, representing to-day the bishops of our country in this cause which interests all of us, to appeal to your faith, to your patriotism and to your spirit of fairness and to beg of you to comply with our request. It is in the name of our bishops, of the hierarchy and of the French Canadian Catholics, that we beg of your party, whose worthy leader you are, to help ns in obtaining a settlement [DOT]of this vexed question, and to settle it by voting with the government in favour of the remedial Bill. We are not asking yon to vote for the government, hut in favour of the measure which will restore to us our rights, and which will he submitted to the House in a few days, etc.
(Signed): A. LACOMBE,
OjM.I.
What shall we say of the stand taken by the leader of the opposition who refused to comply, who continued his agitation, the outcome of which was the defeat of the conservatives in 1896, but also the wiping out of the rights of our compatriots in the province of Manitoba?
With a political record such as the one I have described, should any reliance be put in the promises and policy of the liberal party? And are they making any promises? No, their party organs are making an onslaught, that is all. That is why I have' riot supported the Laurier amendment, and rightly so, as it was not serious.
^ Times have changed since the days when the two governments who are responsible for the passing and sanctioning of that unjust legislation of 1890 were holding the reins of power; both of them are now in their political grave. The distinguished gentleman who is now at the head of the Manitoba government is very well disposed, and we have every reason to depend on his faithfulness for which his record is sufficient pledge, while Sir Wilfrid Laurier had to deal with a fanatical government made up of his allies, and very badly inspired. Under such conditions failure was inevitable. Todhy, having dealt justly with Manitoba, having enlarged its frontiers, having granted the amounts request-

ed as subsidies, we expect from that province, not favours, but full and entire justice for our compatriots, and we shall be greatly disappointed if we fail in obtaining that.
I lay down as a principle that it is but fair that we should add that territory to this little province. After all, Keewatin is made a part of Manitoba with all her rights to the very act by which this province has been constituted, rights which have been trodden upon by Greenway's liberal government, but which still exist, having been ratified by the judgment of the Privy Council, and shall not cease to be claimed until they have been acknowledged'. Those same Tights exist for Keewatin and nothing but a new and nefarious legislation such as was adopted in 1890, could paralyse them if not absorb them and make them disappear. If this should happen, the same recourse to the federal parliament still exists as in 1896, for this territory, as it did exist for Manitoba, and were w<e even to add1 clauses after clauses in order to guarantee the rights to separate schools we would be doing no more than to pour ink upon paper, than to deliver a great many useless speeches if we are dealing with intransigent and unjust people.
But no. We expect something better on the part of Manitoba. The wave of intolerance that has dashed upon that province in 1890, stirred up as it was. by the friends of the leader of the opposition, is lulling from day to day. The example of justice and equity whicn is set constantly by the province of Quebec impassible though she has to face this profligacy of fanatism shall, at last, make our compatriots of a different language and creed understand that the time ot moral and religious slavery must be over;, that the Catholics and the French must be granted the full measure of liberty to which they are entitled in this land of Canada. Shall we, the sons of those valiant knigihts who have discovered' the plains of the West; shall we, the brothers of tnose missionaries who have shed their blood on this territory of Canada, keep waiting in vam for a glimpse of liberty? Loudly do we beseech the province of Manitoba to open her doors wide open and make us Dreathe, at last, that liberty, a glorious attribute of the British flag.
From that day only shau we have peace in our country. One may check, one may restrain the exercise of a right for a time, for a long time even, but one cannot make it perish when it rests upon the Eolid basis of justice and of equity. I would ask my English-speaking compatriots who represent all parts of Canada, to repeat these words Mr. BOULAY.
to their electors: The day when the French language would cease to be written and spoken in this part of America which is called Canada, that day would mark the destruction and the ruin of the British flag, for, as somebody has so well said it before me, the last shot that shall be fired for the preservation of this country in behalf of the British crown shall be, fired by a French Canadian.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the question of extending the Manitoba boundaries is a very important one, and there is nothing strange in the fact that the measure now under consideration has given rise to a most interesting debate.
There could be and there is, in fact, no serious objection to extending the territory of Manitoba itself as far as the shores of Hudson bay. It is admitted by the whole population of this country that it is only fair and just that the territory of Manitoba should be extended; both political parties have given their entire adhesion to this project.
' Of course, the building of a railway up to Hudson's Bay, which has been resorted to as a new element for the solution of the transportation problem shall be of great help towards developing that region through industrial, agricultural and commercial channels. But while the proposition itself of annexing Keewatin to 'Manitoba meets
with no opposition, quite the reverse can be said of the conditions attached to the cession. Protests have been made in all parts of the country against the exorbitant advantages which Manitoba was granted from a financial point of view. The people of this country will hardly understand and will surely blame the decision arrived at by the cabinet as regards the payment of certain arrears. In fact, how is it possible to explain that a certain sum of $2,178,000 is paid to Manitoba as arrears? True it is that negotiations have been carried on more or less assiduously for a few years past, but they have been pushed to an end only of late, when Mr. Roblin, after a conference with his friends of the Borden government, left again for Winnipeg, crying out victory. And he had good reasons for crying out victory, owing to the guilty compliance and to the excessive generosity of the government, he had just been granted, besides Keewatin, a yearly increase of subsidy of about $516,000. Nay more-and this seems to be beyond all limits-the federal ministers count that subsidy from four years back, and at once, they pay over to Manitoba $2,178,000. Is it strange that protests are made and.they grow louder everywhere?
We claim that such preference, if it brings Mr. Roblin super-abundant joy, is unjust towards all the other provinces of the Dominion and that they will soon ask ito share in that god-send with the Manitoba lion.
On the other hand, astonishment and then indignation have seized upon groups which, up to this day had shown themselves in close sympathy with the cabinet, and particularly with the French Canadian ministers. In the province of Quebec a good many spheres of society are pervaded with astonishment and indignation. It is found strange that there is not in the Bill before the House about the Manitoba boundaries a clause regulating education in the territory which is being annexed. They feel indignant when thinking that the so-called knights without fear or reproach who they were formerly, even up to yesterday, the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel), would have flinched, would have failed to their word, would have been so weak, in short, as to violate their solemn pledges of last election.
For my part, having been for fifteen years the constant witness of all the plots and denunciations of those ministers, I readily understand if I do not share entirely the indignation of the sincere and honest people who, in certain quarters, raised their admiration to the point of adulation. Yes, I understand it especially well when I con-

sider the admission of importance which they have just made to the House with so oratorical precautions and endless quotations of statutes more or less contradictory. I understand it and I explain it to myself when I remember the appeals made to prejudice by the Conservative party, especially at the time the Manitoba school question was settled, in 1896. We remember that in 1896 and in 1898, the party under the direction of the right, hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads the opposition to-day was exposed to the attacks of those who, to-day hold portfolios in the Borden administration, and of Mr. Bergeron who, at that time, occupied an eminent position in his party.
What did those devoted champions of integral right in educational matters then pretend? They said that the rights of Catholics in school matters had been sacrificed by the Laurier government in the Manitoba school settlement. It was then that Mr. Bergeron discovered that sir Wilfrid Laurier was not Catholic enough and that there had been no Manitoba school settlement. Strange to say, Mr. Bourassa, far from approving of the stand thus taken, thought that Mr. Bergeron was too Catholic and when naming Mr. Bergeron, I also include those who were then his followers in the federal arena, Messrs. Monk, Pelletier and Nantel.
Would the House kindly accompany me for a moment while I go through the parliamentary debates of 1908? At a certain moment, Mr. Bergeron and Mr. Bourassa join issue on the school settlement and in order not to trespass upon the indulgence of this House by dwelling too long on a worn out topic, let me quote the very words uttered by the member for Labelle, such as reported in ' Hansard ' of that year. About the Laurier-Greenway school settlement, Mr. Bourassa said:
' When they came into power, the Laurier government had to deal with that ticklish question so as to give substantial justice to all parties, without deceiving anybody, and that is what they did. I do not wish to stir up past quarrels.'
Let me tell you here, Mr. Speaker, how all friends of peace and harmony in this country admired those words in 1898. Air Bourassa was brought to book by the very men who now seem to be slumbering in the delights of power. The hon. the Postmaster General above all, then stormed in the Province of Quebec against what he called Sir Wilfrid's shameful capitulation.
Is it to be wondered at if the hon. the Minister of Public Works, the Postmaster General and the Minister of Inland Revenue should reap the storm in the verv province where they have sown the wind of prejudices and passions?

I do not want to take up to no purpose the time of this House by going into all the details of the charges and accusations and denunciations piled up on the head of the venerable leader of the Liberal party during the elections of 1900 and 1904, in connection with this same Manitoba school question.
But it was in 1905; when the two provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were created that the rage of the gentlemen who now occupy the treasury branches reached its paroxysm. Language, creed, race, everything was offered up in sacrifice to the ogre of Orangeism. The hon. gentlemen who then occupied seats in this House still have a vivid recollection of the phillipics delivered by the conservative members a" well as of the nebulous harangue of the hon. member for Jacques-Cartier (Mr. Alonk). What is most to be wondered at is that the hon. gentleman denounced the government because they had yielded on clause 16 No. 1, and yet, he confessed, during the debate, that the text substituted to that clause was clearer more explicit and therefore more favourable to the minority.
On the 23rd Alarch, 1905, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) is reported (page 3193 'Hansard') as follows:
So, I do not see in the last enactment that there is any concession-very far from it. I think the last amendment goes perhaps ft little farther than the original enactment which caused so much excitement, because it defines more clearly what the privileges of the separate schools are. They were not defined at all in the original enactment. It defines them by the reference to the chapters of the Northwest Ordinances where they are fully explained, so that it defines more clearly these privileges, and it may he argued that it secures to the separate schools the right of religious instruction.
Here we have the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) giving the preference to the substituted text over the former clause. And yet he contrives to denounce the Laurier govern, ment, because the measure of school privileges dealt out to the two new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan was not deemed adequate. As a result there was a wide-spread agitation throughout the province of Quebec and Mr. Monk was everywhere acclaimed as the champion of Catholic rights. Let us pass over the elections of 1908 in order to reach those of 1910 and 1911.
Twice in 1910 and quite recently in 1911, at the beginning of this session, did the hon. the Minister of Public Works charge the right hon. the leader of the opposition with having sacrificed the rights of his coreligionists during the last fifteen years. He has upon each occasion, maintained

that on account of his so-called weaknesses, Sir Wilfrid Laurier had forfeited the confidence of his co-religionists.
Now what is the present situation?
Hardly have six months elapsed and events have just sided with the right hon. gentleman so bitterly denounced by the hon. minister. The system of compromise and conciliation so bitterly denounced has become the watch-word of the new minister.
Formerly, in imitation of the American patriot, Patrick Henry, the hon. gentleman and his French Canadian colleagues used to exclaim while appealing to us:
' You may accept fetters, if you like, as for us, we say: Freedom or Death! ' But they have somewhat altered the libretto; and now they sing in chorus, 'ddlcissimo''; 'O school freedom, thou art but a name!' Let us confine ourselves to the sweets of office".
If that is what the ministers say ' sotto voce ', in a whisper, what do they say, when speaking aloud before parliament?
As a matter of fact, the question before the House provides for the annexation of Keewatin to Manitoba and in that Bill you cannot find a single clause defining the privileges of the minority in educational matters. Every one is wondering and asking how the hon. the Minister of Public Works and his three Catholdc colleagues in the Borden cabinet could explain away the absence of that clause.
However amazing it may appear, the hon. the Minister of Public Works, says that there is no school rights in Keewatin and I shall by and by give a few extracts from his speech.
As to the hon. the Postmaster General, in a great display of oratory, he has found out that practically there are no Catholics in Keewatin, a handful at most; that, should there happen to be any Catholics there, they have no vested educational rights, and finally supposing that they had rights they have never asserted those rights.
As will be seen, he dismisses quite un-cermoniously the claims of their friends who so faithfully supported them at the last election.
The hon. the Minister of Justice thinks that he would be very foolish, were he to jeopardize the fat important portfolio which he is now holding, and the hon. the Minister of Inland Revenue, (Mr. Nantel), not unlike the fourth officer in the famous burial of Malborough, simply keeps mum.
Would you like to know what has resulted from the painful partition of the hon. Minister of Public Works, in connection with school matters, on this Manitoba Boundaries Extension Act?
In the first place, a denial of all the rights of the minority.
Let us listen to the Minister of Public Works, (page 4630, unrevised ' Hansard '):
The provision is reproduced in the statutes of 1896, hut it never was in any way enforced in the district of Keewatin. This Act of 1875 never applied to the district of Keewatin in any way.
And further on (page 4638)
I have said to the House that in my estimation there are, in this territory, no vested rights, no substantial rights acquired under any legislation.
And further on again, page 4641, answering a question which he had been asked by the hon. gentleman from Two-Mountains fiMr. Ethier), with regard to the vested rights

The difference is this, that the rights of the Hudson Bay Company are purely proprietary rights, os to which there is no doubt whatever, and in transferring this territory, we are obliged to provide for those proprietary rights. I do not think there are any vested educational rights, but if there were any, the only way in which they could be protected, if the transfer is to take place, is under the educational clause 22 of the Manitoba Act, which we cannot change or vary in any way.
Again, page 4632 replying to this question of the right hon. the leader of the opposition! Sir Wilfrid' Laurier): Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that there are no such rights?"

I am certainly of opinion, and have endeavoured to show, that there are no rights of any kind existing.
At last, page 4637:
Then, there were no vested rights of any kind in Keewatin territory, and there are at present no vested rights, nothing substantial in the way of legal or acquired rights in the territory with which we are dealing.
At all events, in the course of his remarks, the hon. Minister of Public Works intimates that the minority would have a shadow of vested rights had ordinances been passed with respect to education. It is true that no ordinance was passed by the commissioned: in council, and on the ground that if there is a commissioner, there is no council.
But the hon. minister informs us that an application from a Catholic bishop had been forwarded to this government with a view to obtaining the appointment of a council which would be authorized, with the commissioner, to pass the ordinances asked for by that bishop and his flock. That demand was not granted and the consequence was that, in the opinion of the hon. minister, the minority has no vested rights.

But who is responsible for this application being denied? The hon. Minister of Public Works, the hon, Postmaster General and the government. It would be of no avail to plead extenuating circumstances.
In this connection the hon. Postmaster General has taken a stand for which he will be severely blamed. He said :
As far as we are concerned I may say that we received a similar request sometime in December last. Those who made that demand were not desirous enough that it should he granted to take the trouble of speaking about it for even five minutes with any of the four Catholic members of this government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how can the hon. the Postmaster General reasonably expect that Mgr. Charlebois or the petitioners will travel 1,600 miles to confer with him? The venerable, bishop sent in his petition -or that of his flock and I am convinced that he did not consider it necessary to undertake a 1,600 mile journey to make the acquaintance of the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) however interesting he may be.
The main point is that the Catholics' petition was ignored.
Whatever may be the opinion expressed by Catholic ministers in the cabinet, whether or not a study of the statutes reveals the clear and undeniable rights of minorities in Keewatin to separate schools, whether or not ordinances were enacted, it none the less remains to be considered whether or not it is opportunte to insert in this Bill a clause defining the status of minorities in annexed territories in educational matters.
In my humble opinion, any provision of that nature, if not accepted beforehand by the government of Manitoba, will be of no effect.
We would probably in any case obtain no better result than that of 1896, at which time the minority obtained recognition of their grievances as against the spoliation measure of 1890, at which time Sir Wilfrid Laurier solved the Manitoba schools difficulty in the only possible and reasonable manner, as admitted by Mr. Bourassa himself.
Have we not in this incident of 1870 the absolute proof that a federal statute however clear may be set at nought by a province? The Manitoba Act (art. 22) secured to Catholics the right to separate schools. The provincial government utterly neglecting this explicit provision, enacted legislation abolishing the separate school system in Manitoba and that law was declared to be constitutional by the highest court of the empire.
Of what value, therefore, is the contention that the only way of securing the school privileges of the minority is to in-Mr. BELAND
sert in the Bill an imperative provision to that effect. For my part, I can perceive but one way of meeting the difficulty now facing us. That means is entirely at the disposal of the government.
Let us first of all take up the British North America Act of 1871, section 3, and then place face to face the two governments concerned in the annexation of Keewatin to Manitoba, and it will be possible to settle the difficulty without firing the train. Let us first of all read clause 3 of the Constitutional Act of 1871:
3. The parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province of the said Dominion, increase, diminish, or otherwise alter the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed to by the said legislature, and may, with the like consent, make provision respecting the effect and operation of any such increase or diminution or alteration of territory in relation to any province affected thereby.
The annexation of any territory to a province is the result of an agreement between the federal government and that of the province interested.
In that agreement are to be found the terms and conditions as finally accepted and stipulated by both parties.
On examining the conditions of the agreement between the governments of Canada and Manitoba with respect to the annexation of Keewatin, I find that the limits of the territory have been defined and that this definition has apparently been accepted by both parties.
It has, I see, been stipulated that certain sums of money shall be paid as arrears and afterwards annually by the federal government to Manitoba, which arrangement also seems to have been agreeable to both parties.
I note also that the vested rights of the Hudson's Bay Company are to be respected, and many other things besides. All of these matters have been arranged by means of conferences.
The Roblin government is friendly towards the Borden government. Would it not have been possible had they taken the trouble for the Catholic ministers in the cabinet to obtain by agreement and with the consent of both parties, the insertion of a clause securing the privileges required by the minority?
This has been done, and I submit to the House that it is the great mistake made by the government. Every attempt to insert any such clause against the will of Manitoba must fail.
The other day my hon. friend from Pie-tou (Mr. Macdonald) put the following question to the Minister of Public Works:
' Has the hon. Minister (Mr. Monk) any

assurance or promise that anything will be done?'
This was with reference to school privileges.
And the minister answered: ' Absolutely none.'
It was clearly the duty of the ministers to insist upon the acceptance of such conditions as appeared essential to the protection of minorities. It [DOT] is not yet too late to do so. Delay the third reading of the Bill and re-open negotiations with Manitoba. You will secure these conditions, you will insert them in the Bill and we shall enact the law containing them. This difficult question can be settled by conciliation only. It may be settled in a satisfactory manner if the Catholic ministers will but display the courage, energy and determination which the people have a right to expect from them.
The Liberal party has always favoured methods of conciliation. Liberals have always refused to resort to coercion measures, because although these may appear more brilliant and in some cases appeal to certain classes, they cannot fail in the end to lead to serious difficulties and even to disastrous results.
But extremists of all shades, who in the absence of a text in support of their contentions, never fail to appeal to the constitution; what are these men doing with the constitution to-day?
They set it aside and they remain in hiding behind a rampart of some twenty statutes; a very fragile one for ail are more or less contradictory, and the fabric, therefore, may easily be overthrown by the slightest wind of public indignation.
In the name of the Catholic population of Keewatin, of Manitoba, and of other provinces of the Canadian confederation; in the interest of peace and harmony between the citizens of this country, I call upon the government not to insist to-day upon the third reading of the Bill. I call upon them to delay it for some time, for one month perhaps, to take up once more negotiations with the government of Manitoba for the purpose of prevailing upon that province to accept of their own volition, as a condition of the annexation of Keewatin, such educational privileges as shall be acceptable to the minorities and concerning which the effect of existing laws may be doubtful.
I have no doubt whatever that such a move would give excellent results, nay I will go further and say that by a step of this kind alone can minority privileges be recognized and protected, because their recognition will be based upon conciliation and an agreement freely consented to by both parties.
Should the government refuse to meet this just demand, should they persist in 157
using their majority to force through the third reading, then they implicitly admit that they hold as of no account the wishes of the majority of citizens in this great country and that they are ready to trample under foot the solemn promises made before the electoral body.
I have the honour to propose that this Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be resolved:
' That this House is of opinion that negotiations should be re-opened with the government of Manitoba in order to define by amicable conferences the status of minorities, either Protestant or Catholic, with regard io education in the light of existing laws in the annexed territory.'

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I could well understand my hon. friend from Yamaska (Mr. Mondou) and my hon. friend from Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche) approaching the discussion of this delicate question from the point of view of their own conscientious conviction and therefore I am only too pleased to consider the views of those hon. gentlemen with feelings of the most profound respect and consideration. But, Mr. Speaker, when my hon. friend (Mr. Beland) moves that the Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to committee, and that we hold a further conference with the government of Manitoba, I say that we cannot even consider the acceptance of this amendment, and I am surprised that my hon. friend who was a member of the late administration during its last days should suggest any such course. The late government on the 22nd of February, 1909, transmitted for the consideration of the government of Manitoba a Bill by which the right hon. gentleman proposed to settle the question which this parliament is now being asked to settle, by giving the present Bill a third reading to-night. In connection with the measure presented to the government of Manitoba, the leader of the opposition did not invite then, and I do not believe he will invite now, any such conference as that proposed by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. Let me read the Bill to which I refer and the letter from the right hon. gentleman which accompanied it. The letter is as follows:
Ottawa, 26th Feb., 1909.
Dear Mr. RobJin,-
I have the honour to enclose the draft of a Bill for the extension of the boundaries of the province of Manitoba. This Bill is on the line of the resolutions adopted by the House of Commons at its last session. The amount of the allowance to be paid to the province in lieu of lands, has been left in *blank. According to the aforesaid reeolu-



tion of the House of Commons, this amount should he fixed iby negotiation between tho Dominion government and the government of the province.
We will be happy to confer with you at any time that may be convenient to yourself and your government.
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd.) WILFRID LAHRIER,
Now I will read the draft of the Bill referred to:
An Act to provide for an increase of the limits of the province of Manitoba.
Whereas a petition has been presented to the House of Commons on behalf of the Legislative Assembly of the province of Manitoba praying, amongst other things for an extension of the boundaries of that province northward and eastward and for an additional subsidy to the province in lieu of the ownership of the public lands in the territory to be added to the province by such extension, and it is expedient to grant the prayer of such petition to the extent and in the manner provided in the enactments hereinafter contained; therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1.	Upon the legislature of the province of Manitoba consenting thereto, the limits of the said province shall be increased so that the northern boundary of the province shall be the sixtieth parallel of north latitude; the western boundary shall be the present eastern boundary of the province of Saskatchewan; the eastern boundary shall be the present eastern boundary of the province to the northeast corner thereof, thence in a straight line to the most easterly point of Island lake and thence in -a straight line to the point where the eighty-ninth meridian of west longitude intersects the shore line of Hudson bay, thence following the said shore line 'to its intersection with the sixtieth parallel;
2.	And whereas in accordance, with the provisions of the Act establishing the province of Manitoba ithe ungranbed lands of the Crown in the territory so to be added to the said province will continue to be administered by the government of Canada foT the purposes of Canada and the province will not have such lands as a source of revenue, it is further enacted that there shall be paid by Canada to the province an increased allowance by money payment to an amount of
The amendment was left blank.
3.	This Act shall come into force upon a date to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me ask the hon. mover of the amendment if he can find one syllable in this Bill that would justify this amendment. Not only was this Bill forwarded to the Premier of Manitoba, but immediately on its receipt a delegation was appointed by the government of the province to come to Ottawa and take up the question of the conference as suggested in Mr. ROGERS.
the letter of the leader of the opposition, and I was honoured by being invited to become one of that delegation. We came to Ottawa and sat in conference for several hours, upon the second and third of the following month, I think, and we discussed everything connected with the settlement of this question, save and except the matter which my hon. friend (Mr. Beland) has brought to the attention of the House tonight. If hon. gentlemen opposite had any idea of asking Manitoba to take any such action as they are suggesting to-night by this amendment, that was the time and that was the place to have made the rerequest. But they did not do so, and therefore, I claim they have no right to urge any such proposition now, because the record of the government of Manitoba does not warrant that course. The government and the people of Manitoba are naturally very sensitive with respect to their position upon this question, because for many long years, they have suffered, as no province in Canada lias suffered, owing to outside interference, and especially the interference of the right hon. gentleman, who leads the opposition. That hon. gentleman told us to-night that he had undertaken to effect a settlement with Manitoba in the year 1907 of which he was proud and satisfied. I want to tell him that that settlement has not satisfied any citizen within the borders of Manitoba, be he Protestant or be he Roman Catholic. That settlement has kept this question as a live and a burning issue before the people of the province. Is the Manitoba government which came into power two years after the so-called settlement had been enacted, entitled to be asked to come down and confer upon the question as suggested in this amendment? I say that the actions of that government have not been such as would justify this House in passing this amendment. I will say further, that during the ten or eleven years that I occupied a position in the Manitoba government we never failed in our duty to endeavour to carry out in the most generous, the most fair, and the most liberal manner, the Act complained of, which was placed on our statute book through the interference of the leader of the opposition, and which is doing an injustice to the people of Manitoba.
During the last eight or nine years, the leader of the government in Manitoba and the members of that administration have been accused time and time again by their opponents of being too generous in their interpretation of the law in regard to the minority of that province. And never upon any occasion, to my knowledge, did that government apologize for that generosity or for the broad spirit in which they administered that law to the advantage and comfort, so far as they possibly could, of the

minority of the province of Manitoba. And, so long as I occupy a position in the public life of this country, I do not propose to be either afraid or ashamed to acknowledge my spirit of fairness and justice in all respects to the minority. And in making this statement I feel I represent the views, the broad spirit and generosity, which exists in the province of Manitoba alike with Roman Catholics and Protestants of all classes. My right hon. friend the leader of the government (Mr. Borden) the other night, told us _ about the splendid spirit that existed in the province of Nova Scotia. I wish to tell my right hon. friend and the members of this House that in no province of Canada can you find a better spirit existing as between the two great races of our country than exists to-day in the province of Manitoba. And I say that it would be a sad day when that good feeling now existing there should be interfered with by such an amendment as the one proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Beland). In that province the people are desirous of going on as they have gome on in the past, in harmony and good fellowship one with the other. And if this parliament takes no action such as that suggested by my hon. friend, I have every confidence in the generosity and in the fair-mindedness of the people in that, province, irrespective of race, creed or nationality, and I am sure that they will do everything in their power to settle the affairs of their province on the lines best calculated to promote good feeling. They will follow a course that will be acceptable to all. And I am sure that if Manitoba is left free to take its own course, the result will be just, fair and reasonable, and will carry satisfaction to all who are interested in the maintenance of harmony and in the settlement of this great question.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. C. ETHIER (Two Mountains).
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing the final act of the farce which the government has just played, and having for its subject the Manitoba boundaries question.
Before it is all over, before the voice of the Ontario Tories has drowned the protests of the minority, sacrificed by those who had sworn to protect it, before the French-speaking ministers have been for the last time sat upon by their Ontario colleagues, before the Nationalist majority in this House repudiate once more their leaders, Armand Lavergne and Henri Bourassa, I deem it my duty to define the stand which I propose to take on this question and to give my opinion regarding the men who were entrusted with the duty of defending the minority previously referred to by me.
I wish to point out the manner in which they have deported themselves in regard to this question. I shall not discuss the prin-,1574
ciple of the Bill, which I approve as regards the location of the proposed boundaries. The financial question in connection with the money grants has been discussed by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and particularly in the shape of amendments which have been negatived by the government supporters.
I cannot imagine what has induced the government to increase the grant to the province of Manitoba, contrarily to the principles embodied in the constitution, thereby ignoring the just claims of the maritime provinces, particularly of the provinces of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, in respect to the Dominion subsidies. Why grant to Manitoba an amount of subsidies out of proportion with her population, as compared wtih the other provinces of the Dominion? Moreover, why grant over two millions to Manitoba in the shape of so-called arrears dating back to 1908, though in the meantime the province of Manitoba did not spend a single cent of her own moneys in the interest of the district of Keewatin and for its benefit, said district having always been up to this day administered at the expense of the Dominion parliament?
Should we consider it as a gift which this government is making to- Mr. Roblin, in view of the Manitoba local elections which, it is rumoured, are to take place shortly? Or should we consider it as a leaven to entice the electors into voting for the Roblin government, in the hope that thereby the minority might be granted some special favours in connection with the school difficulties, as suggested by the Postmaster General in his last speech?
But enough has been said in regard to this financial question which, to my mind, is of secondary importance; I wish to deal more particularly with that aspect of the question in which we are most interested, not only we of the province of Quebec, but all members of the minority in this gTeat Dominion, I mean the school question in the territory of Keewatin, which is to be annexed to the old province of Manitoba.
After listening to the explanations given by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) and the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), and even the hon. Minister of Justice, all representing the rights of the minority, I had reason to believe that the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel) would rise in his seat to protest against the stand taken by his colleagues, comparing his present stand with his past utterances. I was anxious to know what his views were since he accepted the portfolio of Minister of Inland Revenue. But I see that he has not as yet opened his mouth, and will not do so; to express the feelings of indignation which should fill his heart

under these circumstances. His views remain ' inland ' in the same way as his portfolio. Silence characterises him since he lias become a minister. However, he was able to speak out previous to September 21, previous to his having a taste of office, of its delights and advantages.
He was still able to speak out when, at St. SchoJastique, on June 24 last (1911), in company with the leader of the hon. Postmaster General and his own Mr. Ar-mand Lavergne, together with Jules Fournier and Jean Prevost, he applauded Mr. Lavergne's spech, and especially the following words uttered before the electors of Two Mountains and Terrebonne: ' See what is going on in our midst, in Manitoba, in Alberta, in Saskatchewan, our religious and national franchises have been sacrificed while we were dozing.'-I imagine it was the hon. Minister of Public Works who was dozing-and, allowing the Lauriers and the Brodeurs to secure honours while losing honour. On this (feast of St. John Baptist, reflect that we have been guilty of such remissness.
On that occasion he applauded the above statements made by Mr. Lavergne, his leader, adding that, if he was elected, and the Conservative party returned to power, he would restore the Separate schools as they were previous to 1890. I know it for a fact, being present at the meeting. The same statement was made at St. Therese de Blainville, in the county of Terrebonne, on September 18th last, three days before polling day'. Mr. Nantel applauded at the time and opened his mouth to exclaim:
' Shame, shame on these traitors! ' But since September 21, he as well as his colleagues, and his colleagues as well as himself, even the hon. Minister of Justice- who, between us, is not content with his salary of Minister of Justice, but retains his pension as former judge-suddenly changed their minds, and like the hon. Minister of Public Works, they said to themselves:
' We are here and you are there,' which means: 'We are in the manger, let us gorge ourselves.'
Subsequent to 1896, the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue stated in the county of Terrebonne and throughout the district, on every public platform, that the Manitoba school question was not settled. In this regard, he is contradicted by the hon. Minister of Public Works, who has just stated, what he had already stated in his former speech, that he had never raised the Manitoba question in public or in this House, in the course of the last fifteen years, as he considered it finally disposed of. At the public meeting of St. Eustache, on July 17, 1910, the Minister of Public Works, while denouncing what he .thought fit to designate as the damnable Navy Act, pledged himself at the same time to re-Mr. ETHIER.-
store the Manitoba schools, and that, with the support of his colleague the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue and of the Nationalist candidate in Two Mountains, Mr. Andre Fauteaux. Such are the pledges given in the province of Quebec.
The hon. Minister of Public Works has certainly not forgotten the statements he made in this House on March 29, 1897, when giving his appreciation of the then Laurier-Greenway agreement, he said: ' I contend that the so-called concessions referred to are worthless.' I consider that the concessions made by the Manitoba government to the Dominion government are paltry and stingy. They are far from being generous. That settlement is a bluff, a gold brick, which will not satisfy any one.
And I affirm that from that date up to the 21st of last September, the hon. Minister of Public Works had the same language during the elections of 1900, 1903, during the by-elections that took place in Two Mountains and Terrebonne; in 1904, 1908 and 1911. He has changed his opinion, but from the day he has become the holder of a minister's portfolio. In order to please the Tory majority of Ontario he has disavowed his past and his programme, he was ashamed of them. And he comes and tells us, with a shocking impudence: The settlement of the school question I have condemned, blamed and censured for fifteen years, but I now approve of it and it is the most effective which could be thought of, under the circumstances.
Those good, faithful and patriotic ministers think of nothing else but drawing their salary, and I have no doubt that the first people to put up an appearance at the accountant's office and to ask for their cheque every month muist be those ministers, those three hirelings who follow in the wake of the Ontario Tory tribe.
The hon. Minister of Public Works has told us that he had not the mania of resignation. That is obvious. He prefers to cling to power in spite of all justice, even in spite of all political decorum.
But let us walk into the Post Office Department. Who is the leader of that department? The hon. L. P. Pelletier. The position he has taken in this debate could be no surprise to any one who knows him; it does not astonish those who have followed his political career for the last twenty-five years. The hon. member for Rouville has portrayed the hon. minister by quoting an extract of his biography which appeared in ' La Croix,' a Catholic newspaper of Montreal and a Conservative newspaper at the. same time. _ What did that paper say about the ministers coming from the province of Quebec, in its edition of the second day of last March? I quote textually. Speaking of the Kee-

watin schools and of the Bill now before us, ' La Croix ' said:
As to the rights of the Catholics of that ter ritor.y to their schools, not a word, not even an allusion.	,
The Borden government ignores them. To his mind they amount to nothing, they do not exist. However, he did not forget to consecrate toy a special clause all the privileges now enjoyed by the Hudson's Bay Company.
If this is not an iniquity perpetrated intentionally, there is no such thing as iniquity.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to interrupt my quotation at .this point and to make a digression about the clause benefiting the Hudson's Bay Company in this Bill. If you remember, Mr. Speaker, upon the second reading of the Bill enacting by clause 7 that the rights of the Hudson's Bay Company should be protected, I asked the hon. Minister of Public Works why the government protected especially the rights of the company and ignored those of the minority, and the hon. Minister of Public Works answered me that clause 7 protected _ the proprietary rights onlly and those rights must be mentioned in the Bill. Now, from the very opening of the present sitting, the right hon. Prime Minister has given notice and has had the said clause 7 crossed out, alleging that it was useless, and this, notwithstanding the opinion of a professor of constitutional law at a certain university of Montreal, the Hon. Mr. Monk, who, in answer to my question, had said the contrary.
In face of this official denial by the Prime Minister as to the opinion of his colleague the Minister of Public Works on a legal question like this, I am not surprised to see that his pupil, the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Mondou), has changed his own opinion of the value and merit of the hon. minister's knowledge as far as constitutional law is concerned.	.
And if his opinion as to the existence of the rights of the minority in the Keewatin district is as doubtful as that which he expressed with respect to the rights of the Hudson's Bay Company and to the necessity of protecting them in this Bill, it is not worth more in the one case than in the other, and I am surprised that his own pupils, even the member for Yamaska, do desert him.
But I shall leave this aside, and come hack to the hon. Postmaster General, and I shall go on making the House acquainted with the sayings of ' La Oroix,' which I was quoting.	[DOT]
Speaking of the present government, this newspaper says further:
They are in power, they have authority, they also have strength; nothing prevents them from acting, their is no obstacle in their way, and still what are they doing?
Impassive like a hangman who has lost all human sentiments, they abandon the Catholics of Keewatin to the torture of neutral schools.
What shall the ministers: Mr. Monk, Mr. Pelletier and Mr. Nantel do?
Shall they throw their portfolios on the table of their chief if he persists in leaving ont of this Bill a clause to the effect of acknowledging the rights of the Catholics of Keewatin to their schools? Have they even insisted on that point, so far? We know nothing of it as yet. The events which are going to occur at the Commons will tell ns.
But from a Pelletier especially, we expect nothing good, nothing manly.
That soul of a politician bent under the yoke of personal interest is nothing good in our estimation.
To resist the craft and the hatred of the lodges, one must not be but a cunning lawyer, he must have a will inclined to do good, a soul which has stood the test of sacrifice, a generous heart, fixed principles; and Mr. Pelletier is devoid of all that.
Oh, I know that the Postmaster General has declared this newspaper to be unworthy of respect. However, when it sang the oraises of these gentlemen previous to the 21st day of last September, and when it abused the right hon. leader of the opposition, it was read with satisfaction. But if this newspaper has ever struck the right note it has certainly done so when speaking of the Postmaster General as it did.
I say that the French ministers follow in the wake of the Tory majority-of Ontario; that it is the voice of Ontario which commands, and I shall quote as ground for such assertion, an impudent article of the * Citizen,' a government organ published in this city. That article appeared this morning, March 12, and here is an extract of it which is very expressive :
Hon. Mr. Borden's government was not affected either by Quebec as a province or by Mr. Bourassa, and possibly the sooner this basic fact is emphasized, the sooner the people of Canada will cease to have their parliamentary business unnecessarily meddled with. In the days of the Laurier government, which lived and moved and had its being by leave of Quebec province, as that province was then represented in parliament, necessarily everything that Quebec thought or felt or said had to receive that attention which is due to a force which can make or unmake a premier. Times have changed. The people of Canada, as a whole, have elected the Borden government with a working majority quite irrespective of the province of Quebec.
And the French ministers keep silent, they swallow this insult without wincing. Did not the Prime Minister himseH say at Toronto, the day after the election which took place on the 21st of September fast, that Ontario haid made heT powerful voice heard? The rights of the minority are being trodden upon, and the hon. Minister of Public Works comes and tells ns that this minority has no rights. It is not strange.

for the hon. Prime Minister himself stated on the very first reading of the Bill, that there were doubts as to the existence or the non-existence of rights in behalf of the minority in Keewatin. If there is a doubt, why then refuse the benefit of it to the minority? Twenty-four members have declared, by their vote, that they claimed the benefit of that doubt in favour of the minority by means of an amendment which was proposed and rejected.
But I bow down to this denial on the part of the majority, because it consecrates for ever the legal right of such majority. They have taken away from us the right which we believed, in good faith, we should claim.	j
Why now does the House refuse to hold out to the minority a sheet-anchor, the last of all, in order to protect their rights, or at least a scrap of those rights, by rejecting the amendment which has been proooscd by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Be-land)?
Why is it that the government and the Prime Minister, who has some doubts, should not agree to submit this question to some expert and disinterested parties, to some distinguished lawyers, to the Supreme Court, for instance, and to the Privy Council if need be?
By the amendment which the hon. member for Beauce has proposed, the government could secure an honourable arrangement with respect to this question. But no, an important question like this breeds hesitation. If some poor employees must be beheaded though not guilty of anything else than being Liberals, then there is no hesitation and the guillotine works regularly.
Now, let us proceed by an analogy. Has the government shown any energy at ail in the case of the Bill which was introduced by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) concerning the Ne Temere decree on marriages in the province of Quebec? If the government has deemed it proper to refer this question to the Supreme Court and even to the Privy Council if need be and this notwithstanding the opinion of the honourable Minister of Justice and of the Prime Minister himself-which opinion has been corroborated by the exMinister of Justice and by Sir Wilfrid-why, on such an important question as the rights of the minority of Keewatin, why not accede to a request of that kind and submit the question to the same judicial authorities, so as to make it a test case? No, Mr. Speaker, the voice of Quebec rules no more, the Tory voice of Ontario is the one which now rules, and as Mr. Bourassa, their past chief, would say, our ministers from Quebec follow those who take them to pasture like sheep. I believe that this latter is sincere because he maintains the posi-Mr. ETHIER.
tion lie has taken with the five other Nationalists whom he got elected, and w-ho have voted in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition on the second reading of the Bill.
I shall not address the House any longer on that question. May I be permitted, however, to add that, in my humble opinion, the idea which has always prevailed with the fathers of confederation from the first, and with the Canadian statesmen who have succeeded one another from Sir John Macdonald up to the present time was: Protection to the mindrity and equal justice to all minorities in the different provinces which compose this vast Dominion? One has only to study the British North America Act of 1867, the laws concerning the admission of the Northwest Territories and of Rupert's Land into confederation, the Territories Act of 1875, the Keewatin Act of 1876, and last, chapter 62 of the Revised Statutes of Canada (1906), to convince one's self that my pretension is well founded in law, whatever the hon. Minister of Public Works may say or think contrarywise.
It is the same as to the Acts concerning Alberta and Saskatchewan and1 has induced me to vote for the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Yamaska.
It may be pointed out that this is in contradiction with my vote on the settlement of the Manitoba sohool question in 1897, but the situation to-day is very different. What I did in 1897, I should" do again under the same circumstances, even as I would be ready to renew my vote in favour of the Mondou resolution without feeling that I had in any way contradicted my past record.
The difference is that in 1897 the question had been pending since six years, going from court to court and from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. When we were returned to power in 1896 the question was exhausted, the life had been taken out of it by the contradictions of the Conservative party who, to use the expression employed by the hon. the Post Master General, had played football with it.
It was the 'Conservative party who, from 1890 to 1896, fostering race and religious prejudice carried us to the verge of civil war. This was by good luck avoided thanks to the diplomacy and the energy of the then Prime Minister, to his policy of peace and conciliation. This indeed was the only practical manner of fettling the question, as onljjtlater admitted by the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), and in 1897 by Mr. Bourassa, as stated by him in reply to the hon. member for Beauharnois, Mr. Bergeron.
To-day the situation is not the same; the matter is just beginning. The opposi-

tion are not responsible for the deeds of the government who act as they deem expedient. Shall this farce which lasted from >1890 to 1896 be repeated?
In a word, and on account of the considerations I have just recalled, I will vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Beauce, because, wanting a better, it is the last and supreme chance offered to the Keewatin minority.
By following the policy of conciliation, concord and peace inaugurated by the hon. leader of the opposition the question may be disposed of for ever and I hope that the five Nationalists who have shown their sincerity so far will vote in favour of the amendment now submitted.

speechtext:
The amendment of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) is based on the same capital error as all the otbes amendments are, it fails to recognize that this proposal, like

the other proposals, is an interference with the sovereignty of the province of Manitoba. We have settled once for all that Manitoba is. sovereign -within her own territory, and any proposal in this House to enter into negotiations with Manitoba over this question would raise the issue that she was not sovereign over this question at the present time. No other province in this country would for a moment entertain a proposal to reconsider her constitutional rights.

speechtext: You can confer with a sovereign.

maintopic: POSITIVE DECLARATIONS OF ' LES CLOCHES' OF ST. BONIFACE.
speechtext:
You may, but this nroposed conference implies that Manitoba is called into court to have her rights readjusted. It is a proposal to reopen a question that has been settled for all time; and if it had not already been settled, I think we must admit that the majority in this House to-night of 136 against the amendment of the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Mondou) has effectually settled it. I remember fifteen years ago when I was in this House and this question first came up, there were eight men in the House who decided to take their political lives in their hands and to say that there should be no coercion of .Manitoba, or any questioning of her rights. I think this majority of 136 votes to-night is a still dearer declaration that there must be no interference with the free action of Manitoba on matters falling within her jurisdiction, and no questioning even of her rights, no invitation to Manitoba to inquire into her rights. I say that the question has been settled once for all, and all we can do now is to write over it ' requiescat in pace.' If this amendment were adopted, some one would then get up in this House and ask Ontario to come into a conference. Would Quebec for one moment consider a proposal that she should go into a conference to have her constitutional rights made the subject of inquiry? Would Ontario do it? Would little Prince Edward Island do it? Certainly not. We must respect the rights of all the provinces in this House, we must leave off discussing them for no good can come of it. For sixteen years now we have had more or less discussion of this question in this House, and to no good purpose. There are other and more important questions before the people that ought to command our attention. If there is to be a conference where should that conference be held? That conference should be held in Manitoba, and it should be held between the minority in Manitoba and the provincial government. If such a conference were held now, and if there are any grievances, I believe they would be Mr. MACLEAN (S. York.)
adjusted. But that is a matter with which we have nothing to do in this House. Every speaker on this question to-day has acknowledged that Manitoba is seized with jurisdiction in this matter, her sovereignty is acknowledged, and no good can come of prolonging this discussion any further. Therefore, I shall have to vote against the amendment of the hon. member for Beauce. because I hold that there should be no coercion of Manitoba, either under the guise of a conference, or by way of direct legislation.
