speechtext:
Yes., they were fine words. I am convinced that today Mr. Lavergne would consider three feet of snow at least necessary to cover the mis-deeds of the government he hailed with such delight.
* I do not desire to give any more quotations; I cannot however pass over the statement made a moment ago by the hon. Minister of Public Works that never since 1897, in this House or out of it, he spoke of the Manitoba school question. The hon. Minister went to the length of declaring that when speakers on the hustings had, in his presence, spoken of this question, he had blamed them for it, stating that as far as he was concerned the question was settled and outside the sphere of politics.
Mr. Speaker, on the 6th August last, in the city of Three Rivers, the hon. Minister of Public Works, in company with Mr. Henri Bourassa, opened the electoral campaign in the Province of Quebec. _
I have here the report of that meeting as published in "Le Devoir", recognized organ of the minister.
This is what Mr. Normand, the conservative candidate said :
Mr. Bureau must render you an account of his conduct in the great questions touching our national life. He must account to you for the Manitoba school question which is not settled irr spite of the statements of those who betrayed onr brothers and which remains now as it was then, an iniquitous and monstrous violation of the natural la.w which permits every man to adore God in the language spoken by his father and mother.
The same day, on the same hustings, in the presence of the hon. Minister of Public Works, the hon. deputy Speaker of this House, the Knight (sans peur et sans re-proche,) as described by 'L'Evenement,' made the following statement.

* The resolutions will go this afternoon if the government is defeated before six o'clock/
These are the words of hon. Robert Rogers in reply to the Nationalist demands for delay in the introduction of the Bill to extend the boundaries of Manitoba.
English-speaking Canada has been waiting many years for this straight talk to Quebec clericals. It stirs the British spirit of Canadians to read such a declaration. We have been accustomed for so long to see our representatives at Ottawa grovelling before the black robes of Quebec, that it seems like the banning of a new era to have a responsible Minister declare the intention of the government to do right regardless of the threats of bishops, priests, or their Nationalist infantry.
It is the voice of a full grown man, in whom courage is the dominant characteristic, not the. expression of a politician who listens to the timid council of the place-hunters.
Hon. Robert Rogers has placed himself on the level taken by Sir John Macdonald when he was urged to pardon Louis Riel the second time. Then as now, thq black frocked priests and bishops of Quebec invaded Ottawa to save the neck of a twice convicted murderer. The old chieftain, who had gone much too far when he pardoned Riel the first time, made up his_ mind that the death penalty should he inflicted. Prom within his cabinet, from the floor of the House, from the episcopal palaces of Quebec, they came pleading and threatening to save the French rebel. It was all useless. The old man, driven into the corner by the fierce attacks, gave his head a characteristic shake as he said:
' Riel shall die, if every dog in Quebec barks at my heels.'
Prom that day until last week when hon. Robert Rogers spoke, there has not been such a display of strength and courage among the ministers at Ottawa. We hope that this determination to resist Quebec will be maintained. Ontario and the other provinces will do justice to the French. But the time has come when they will no longer allow Quebec

to ride rough shod over their constitutional rights.
I will not stoop to disprove the malignant charges of that paper against the clergy of the province of Quebec, passing over them in scorn is the best answer which can be given.
But are not the victorious clamours of the organ of this section, whose influence in the administration of the day cannot be denied, a most evident proof of the shameful retreat and the unconditional surrender of the representatives of the minority in the government?
The ministers are complaining bitterly of their Nationalist auxiliaries who to-day are up in arms against them. Their tranquility has been troubled. They lament over the obtrusive voices that disturb their sleep and dispel their dreams.
We can afford to look with indifference on this family quarrel. We have no sympathy for those by whom we have been slandered, hissed and insulted.
We cannot forget that we have been charged with cowardice and treason, when we had done our duty as loyal citizens and had taken our political lives in our hands to stand by a cause which we considered to be in the interest of the country.
Those men, our most violent enemies of yesterday, are to-day isolated, standing between two seats, denounced on the right, ignored on the left, in that position in a word, in which must inevitably sooner or later, find themselves all those who play such a game.
In concluding, I-will say that the stand of the government on this question is the same that they have taken on all the problems they had to solve. They are satisfied with having the agitation kept up and they carefully avoid taking action.
What did we see three or four weeks ago? The ministers from the province of Quebec, the so-called champions of orthodoxy, those lofty sponsors of our religion, in order to please their allies of Ontario who have made a political machine of the ' Ne temere decree,' asking the Privy council in England if they can refrain the province of Quebec from giving effect to the rules of the Catholic church for the oelebration of marriages between members of that faith, instead of voting down at once the arbitrary Bill which had been submitted to the House.
And what about the naval question? It has been solemnly declared in front of every chuch in the province of Quebec that the naval law would be repealed at the first session of Parliament, after the election.
But to-day, the government are waiting to consult with the admiralty and we can easily forecast what the answer will be.

In the meantime we have entered the fight and we will keep' it up to the end.
Public opinion is better enlightened, better informed and conscious of the grave error committed in a moment of weakness is already beginning to regain its foothold. When the occasion will come, the people-will take revenge'on those by whom they have been so outrageously misled.
I will have great pleasure in voting for the amendment of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland).

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, at this late hour of the night and at this phase of the debate,, it is not my intention to detain the House by a long speech, but 1 think it is my duty to give some explanation before casting my vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland).
It has been my privilege for several years past to be acquainted with the ex Postmaster General. I am quite ready to concede here, as I have done more than once outside of this House, that my hon. friend is a talented French-Canadian; nevertheless, I hold together with several members to whom I have spoken about it, that the hon. gentleman, besides being a clever young man is also an excellent comedian. I followed him in that memorable campaign of Drummond-Arthabaska, in the fall of 1909; I followed him during the last electoral fight that was ended by the great victory of the 21st September. On all occasions it was made apparent to me. . .
Is my hon. friend alluding to me?

No. I f m alluding to the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Beland); if I mistake not, my hon. friend must be styled the ex-minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I have always found my hon. friend-he has been a Minister for thirty days-to be very clever when meeting his opponents and discussing thn naval question. I was honoured by his presence in my county and I listened to him on numerous other occasions. When he was addressing French Canadian electors in the province of Quebec, he used to say: Our opponents are trying to work you up about that navy, a small little navy that will serve only to protect your butter and your cheese; you are not going to vote for the large navy that Borden wants, and don't forget that Borden wants to give, besides, 25 million dollars to assist England in the wars of the empire. He invariably concluded in appealing thus to hi3 fellow citizens: If you vote for Laurier, you are voting for a small navy; if you vote for Borden you are voting for a large navy. For him the whole question was between a small and a large

navy. That tactic was clever enough and was fairly successful in several places; it succeeded even in my county, but not sufficiently to prevent my being elected.
To-night, after the vote, I listened with great pleasure, as I always do to, the speech of the hon. member for Beauce, who is one of the best speakers of the province of Quebec.
For more than a week now, we are discussing this question of the Manitoba boundaries. For my part, I took on that question a stand which is absolutely sincere and definite, and that stand I have taken at a considerable sacrifice. For the last ten years, unfortunately, I have been mixed up in politics and I have always fought for the Conservative party in the province of Quebec, in its darkest days, and a few months after taking my seat in this House, I came to the conclusion that I was in duty bound to vote against the party for which I have always fought.
_ I say that it was a great sacrifice. I did it in order to harmonize my vote with my past record and in justice to those whom my conscience called upon me to support under the circumstances.
The hon. member for Beauce has followed the whole debate; he did not however take any part in the discussion upon the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Yamaska. He proposed nothing himself as a measure of justice to the Catholic minority of Keewatin. He now comes forward with a motion having no bearing whatever on the question and which, as he says, would place the rights of that minority in the hands of a few persons who would confer with the government of Manitoba. What would take place at such a conference? Would the hon. member be there? Would I or other members of this House be there to offer suggestions? Certainly not. I say therefore that it is here in this House where the members from the province of Quebec and for all Canada are present that suggestions should be made. If the hon. member will submit a measure calculated to_ protect all the rights of the Keewatin minority, I will undertake to vote with [DOT]him and once more against my party. But I will have none of the measure he now suggests, because I do not believe in its efficacy and past events strengthen me in that connection.
In 1905, the parliament of 'Canada had to debate a question concerning which public opinion was roused as it is to-day. The Liberal government having decided to create two new provinces in the west, Alberta and Saskatchewan, there arose the questions of separate schools and of the preservation of the rights of the French language in those provinces. What took place then? Mr. Bergeron, then member
for Beauharnois, submitted an amendment which reads as follows at page 9046 of the Debates of that year:
That all the words after ' he ' at the end of the question be left out and the words:
' Recommitted to a community of the whole House with instruction that they have power to amend the same by striking out all the words of clause 16 and to substitute therefor the following:
16. Section 93 of the B.N.A.. Act of 1867 shall apply to the said province as if at the date fixed for the coming into force of this Act, the territory included in the said province were already a province, the word ' union ' in the section meaning the same date.
2. The legislature shall have the right to pass laws with reference to education, but it shall always provide for (a) the existence of separate schools and their enjoyment by the minority, Protestant or Catholic, who may claim them, (b) The effective control of said school in matters of teaching by the said minority, (c) the full liberty for the majority in any school district to have such schools as they may desire, (d) the equitable and proportionate distribution between the majority and the minority of all monies appropriated for education by the legislature of the province and of all monies arising from the school fund established by the Dominion Lands Act.
Such is Mr. Bergeron's amendment, it is clear and precise and if the member for Beauce will prepare a similar one to secure the complete protection of the rights of the minority in Keewatin, I solemnly promise to vote for such an amendment.
What took place in 1905? When the division took place on Mr. Bergeron's amendment, the hon. member for Two-Mountains (Mr. Ethier), the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Belaud), and all the French Canadian Liberals from the province of Quebec voted against it. Such is the measure of their sincerity in the protection of the minority and of Catholics in the new provinces. Am I not right in saying that they stand condemned by their past record and they will remain so condemned in the province of Quebec.? At the same period and during the same debate, Mr. Bourassa presented an amertdment concerning education in the new provinces. What did these members do about it? Consult the debates and you will find that they voted against the Catholic minority sacrificing all that they lay claim to today in the name of Catholics of the province of Quebec.	-
Did not the hon. member for Beauce who a moment ago,took upon himself to speak in the name of 42 per cent of the population, vote with his colleagues on your left against the use and maintenance of the French language in the new provinces?
Mr. Speaker, as I have already stated, I have come here resolved to do my duty. I remember the declaration I have made

in the province of Quebec since I am in political life. At the beginning of the present session, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), a talented French Canadian, an honour to his nationality and whom I much admire-quoted certain words he said were uttered by the member for Dorchester, concerning the navy and which appeared to be an attack against the English of Ontario. I deny absolutely having ever uttered the words attributed to, me by the member for Rouville. What I said outside of this Chamber I am ready to repeat here. Some days ago, I gave notice of a motion concerning the navy; I knew what I was doing on that occasion. Somebody had to bell the cat and I did so without hesitation.
I am quite satisfied with the government's attitude on this question, but here again as on the school question, my conduct was entirely sincere, I had no other object butj to do my duty to the best of my knowledge and ability, and notwithstanding the deep regret that I felt and expressed, I did not hesitate to differ from my party, nor shall I hesitate to do in future if I consider it necessary. Let the hop. members for Beauce, Two-Mountains and Kamouraska submit an amendment securing the rights of the minority in Keewatin and I shall be very happy to separate once more from my party and to do my duty. But I refuse to be duped by such people who are not sincere, as I have proved, and for that reason I shall vote against the amendment presented by the member for Beauce.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. B. NANTEL (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, at this advanced hour of the night, I have no intention of making a long speech. Other occasions will offer when I will be able to discuss the question before the people.
I simply desire to call attention to a statement made 'by the hon. member for Two-Mountains, my neighbour, who said that I had promised to settled the Manitoba school question if the Conservative party was returned.
This statement was quite unfounded and I protest strongly against it.
It is true that I have undertaken campaigns on that question, especially in 1896, when I supported in the county of Terrebonne Mr. Chauivin, a devoted partisan of the Manitoban minority. I discovered then to my regret that the electors of the province of Quebec declared themselves favourable to Mr. Laurier against the Remedial Bill. I discovered since that this feeling in favour of the present leader of the opposition did not cease to grow. So much so that approval came to him from quarters whence we had^ at first been encouraged to fight against him. I remember that my friend Mr. Chanvin was twitted with being Mr. SEVIGNY.
more Catholic than the Pope. This was said by Liberal speakers throughout the province of Quebec. I might quote many speeches and newspaper articles in support of what I have said. I will quote only one. It shows clearly that the feeling in favour of Mr. Laurier's school policy had gathered strength and that starting from the deepest strata of the popular conscience it had reached the highest sphere of the religious world.
Allow me to read a despatch published by "Le Soleil" and reproduced by "Le Canada " on the 5th July 1907; it shows that the Laurier-Greenway settlement was then accepted as an accomplished fact.
' Le Canada,' a daily newspaper of Montreal, Sir Wilfrid's organ, reproduced to-day, (July 5, page 8), under the heading ' Sir Wilfrid at Rome,' the following from ' Le Soleil,' organ of Sir Wilfrid, at Quebec:
(Special correspondence.)
Sir Wilfrid, as the despatches have already informed you, spent a few days at Rome, coming from Marseilles by way of Cannes and Genoa.
He was received most courteously by His Holiness Pius X in a private audience.
He was given a reception at the Canadian college, at which were present a number of bishops and prelates.
The speech of His Eminence Cardinal (Vincent) Vanutelli was much remarked. His Eminence complimented Sir Wilfrid on his brilliant qualities as a stateman, and warmly thanked him for the services he had ren-defed to the church.
He spoke of the good example given by Sir Wilfrid Laurier to his fellow citizens in his private life.
The church, he added, is proud of this son of hers who has become, without betraying his convictions or principles the chief magistrate of a great country in which the majority of citizens are Protestants.
I send you without comment these declara/-tions of Cardinal Vanutelli which received prolonged applause from the distinguished audience.
An event such as this taking place after the lame settlement of the school question in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan at length convinced me that the struggle was useless.
Moreover I had still present in my mind the manner in which the champions of the minority had been treated by the electorate of the province of Quebec. The defeat of the Tupper Government, that of onr fellow countrymen Messrs. Taillon, Desjardins, Angers and several others proved to me that popular feeling was swayed by principles different from those we defended.
We might thenceforth say to our compatriots : "Since yon allow yourselves to be blinded in his manner, I do not see why we should insist upon defending principles which you have rejected notwithstanding onr efforts." And when I speak of blindness, I am using a very mild expression as.

some others more appropriate might not be parliamentary.
Thenceforth my mind was made up. I ceased to pay any attention to the Manitoba school question and from that date I have never made any statement of. a nature to justify the words which the hon. member for Two-Mountains has just uttered.
I have been called to task for my silence in the course of this debate, but I had an excellent reason for remaining so. On this point I had taken the lead of my colleagues, Before the Bill now being considered was submitted to the House, I had taken a well defined attitude with respect to the rights of minorities in the West. At a banquet given to the hon. Postmaster General at Quebec, some days before the cabinet was formed, I -had expressed my views.
I have nothing -to add or to withdraw of what I s-aid on that occasion. Nothing since then has altered my views and I stand ready to answer for them before my constituents. I take my full share of ministerial responsibility as to the Manitoba Bound-ries Bill.
As to the Keewatin question, it w-oul-d be useless for me to go into it at any length; it is exhausted. The House has heard all the arguments for and against the adoption of the Bill and the position taken by the government needs no further support.
I will merely call attention to the fact that there would be no justice in imposing upon -Manitoba for the annexation of Keewatin restrictions which nobody dreams of putting upon Quebec for the annexation of Ungava or upon Ontario for the annexation of another portion of Keewatin. Everybody admits that by the fact of this annexation the laws of Quebec, be they school laws or otherwise, become those of Ungava.
In the -case of Manitoba -objection is taken to the school laws of that province under the Laurier-Greenway settlement. But thi-s settlement is after all but an accident to which the -people -o-f Manitoba may themselves apply a remedy. In fact, the Laurier-Greenway settlement cannot be altered by federal legislation. It is unjust in respect to the Catholic minority, but may be corrected by an act of the Manitoba legislature. From this source alone can the remedy come and from the past conduct of the Roblin government there is a moral guarantee that all hope is not at an end and that the province of Manitoba is gradually reverting to a sounder interpretation of the constitution. Besides to whom are due these school difficulties of which we are to-day feeling the full weight?
To such men -as Messrs. Greenway and Sift-on who were rewarded by Mr. Laurier after having cooperated with him in perpetrating the injustice from which the Catholics of Manitoba have suffered so long.
That the system of toleration that n-ow obtains in the province shpuld -be maintained that it gives us hope of a measure of complete justice is established from the declarations just now made by the hon. Mr. Rogers.
I will say no more; I merely wi-shed to deny the statements made by the hon. member for Two-Mountains. I deny once more and in .the most positive manner that I said anything like what he attributed to me. I stand iby what I declared at Quebec. I assume entire responsibility for the attitude I have taken to-night and I have no fear of meeting my constituents on this question. For my part, I -have received no petitions from my county and I do not consider that in acting as I do, I am -abusing of the freedom of action thus left in my hands.
I shall vote ag-ains-t the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Beauce and in favour of the bill which I -consider to be an act of justice towards Manitoba, granting as it does a,ll_proper security to minorities and tending to promote a proper understanding, peace and union between the different races- -and icreeds, whose every right the government is anxious to recognize in an equal measure.

(Translation.) At this advanced hour Mr. Speaker, I will only s-ay a few words upon the question now before us, which is the annexation of the territory of Keewatin to Manitoba at the latter's request. Although I have no intention to consider the Bill from its financial aspect,. I must say that from what I have heard of the debate on that point, I must come to the conclusion that Manitoba has been treated like a favoured -child by this present government; Canada's other -children, will after this, it seems to -me, have much difficulty in believing that parental affection is equally distributed throughout the family. The consequ-en-ce of the government's action, in any opinion, will b-e that other provinces will be coming to us for better terms which w-e will be obliged to grant them if we would wish to preserve that peace and harmony so necessary to progress and to the development o-f the -country. -Such a policy does not tend towards the unification of the different portions of the Dominion. On the contrary it cannot fail to strengthen the secession -movement already becoming apparent.
My intention in rising -this evening is more -especially to touch upon another aspect of the -question; the attitude of the Catholic Conservative members from the province of Quebec.
We have here a Bill for the annexation of territory to one of the provinces of the Dominion. It appears to -me perfectly clear that this territory is at present govern-

ed by laws providing lor the establishment of separate schools. Four members of the government are Catholics from the province of Quebec. Those ministers have proclaimed themselves or have been proclaimed the only true defenders of the rights of minorities. They have abused the Liberal ministers and members, or allowed them to be abused by their stumpers and newspapers, accusing them of being sold, cowards and traitors to their race and religion, in consequence of the attitude of the Liberal party on the question of schools in Alberta, Saskatchewan and /Manitoba. Nay more, one of these ministers the hon. Ministers of Public Works, carried his zeal in the cause of minorities to the extent of demanding the use of the French language in Alberta and Saskat-cbewan, although no statute could be found to support his contention.	_
All or nearly all the French-Canadian members sitting on the Speaker s right and supporting 'the present government were elected as Nationalists, that is to say as champions of the rights of minorities, having specially promised the people that the greivan-oes of our fellow countrymen in Manitoba would be remedied, declaring -everywhere that the school question was not settled and was not as they said dead and buried, that Laurier had nobody left to betray, having betrayed his brothers from the west and Manitoba.
'Elect us/ they said, 'and you will find that all this injustice will -disappear.' 'Alas! what a cruel awakening for the trusting souls who believed them.
In vain had w-e repeated that such declarations were not sincere and that dem-agogism in its worst form was being use-d t-o attain power; in vain did we -explain that the government had done the best it could under the circumstances and that no -other government could have -done as well. The people are now in a position to judge between us. The Bill is before us, but in what manner are the rights of minorities secured? Where are th-e defenders of Catholic rights in the west? Have they withdrawn from the government? Will those who may have done so at one stage cease to support an administration unfaithful to its promises and which refuses to accept their views on a question that should be for them primordial and vital, being the fundamental principle of their policy, as explained to the electorate of Quebec. Are they trying or will they try to defeat the government? No, they will continue to support the present government; we are safe in predicting that, knowing them as we do. But the day of reckoning will -come, and we await it eagerly and confidently.
What has been done to-day by those men who, as the hon. Minister of Public Mr. DEMERS.
Works, said at Nicolet, (I quote from the report of ' Le Devoir ', June 16, 1911):
Parliament has reached suoh a state of degradation and servility, as everybody knows, that the deliberative character of the House is a thing of the past. No deliberation is possible without freedom of -opinion. But such freedom -may be said to be non-existent, especially among members of the majority. They are held fast by the chains of party discipline. When the will of the government has been made known, woe betide any partisan who attempts to disobey the orders of the whip. There remains to him no alternative but to commit * hari-kari/ as the Japanese say, he must commit suicide- publicly. (We m-ay be quite sure that the hon. Minister will never commit ' hari-kari'). This party rule is at the present moment one of the most formidable menaces to our liberty and that of the country, other people are aware of it. And I hope that you will elect, at least with- our help, only such men as are resolved -to throw off that yoke which has become a serious danger to our country and to vote under every circumstance according to their conscience and regardless of that discipline which is admittedly shameful, reducing as it does to impotence the assembly which governs our distinies. When the common good requires it, we must be able to sacrifice personal interests and forget party divisions in deference to the supreme interests of the nation.
What have such men as the hon. the Postmaster General done? I quote from ' L'Action Sociale ' of the 11th September, 1911.
' I am old enough to use my own judgment and I stand by the policy of Monk, Bourassa and Lavergne.' and added ' L'Action -Sociale/ '-that answer was applauded/
Where are the men, such as an hon. French Canadian Conservative member whom I cannot name under the circums-. tanoes and on account of the rules of the House who said, I quote from ' Le Devoir/ 19th June, 1911, report of the Sorel meeting:
On the other hand, while Mr. Lemieux said that the rights of the French language in the West must be abandoned, Mr. Monk stood for the complete exercioe of those rights, and Mr. Borden, convinced that the French language was not guaranteed by the constitution, refusing to listen to the claims set forth by his colleague, Mr. Monk broke away from his party; and thus meeting from the extremities of partisanship Mr. Monk and Mr. Bourassa clasped hands. That alliance will certainly some day bear fruit, and today, says Mr	 we are definitely '
seperated from the parties	
It will be asked: Who shall lead this free and independent movement. It matters little,
says Mr	Give us independent
members in the House, give us good soldiers
and leader will appear	 Of course,
these also will follow political leaders, but on condition that they shall defend the rights of the Catholic religion and of the French language.

And what does the hon. member for L'lslet- think of all this? Will he continue to support the present government, and the Minister of Public Works, he who stated at the Fraserville meeting (I quote from 'Le Devoir's' report of that meeting):
He recalled the memorable days of 1905, when being then a new member of the House, the first voice he heard raised in favour of our brothers in the West, was that of Mr. Bourassa, who, with his friend, Mr. Lavergne, extended his hand over party barriers to Mr. Monk and his few disciples in order to defend.those whose rights were denied.
And to-day, once more, we inscribe upon our programme: Justice to ithe French language.
And what does the hon. member for Jo-liette think of 'his chief Mr. Monk' as he said, with emphasis, no doubt, on the 26th August, 1911 ('Le Devoir', 29th August, 1911)? Will he continue to support the present government which has been found wanting upon what he declared to be the only, the great question?
What do the electors of the province of Quebec think to-day when they remember having read and heard the words uttered by Mr. Normand, Conservative-Nationalist-opposition candidate in Three-Rivers (Report by 'Le Devoir', 7th August 1911 of the meeting held at Three-Rivers the 6th)?
You have come, he said, to call Mr. Bureau to account for his stand on those great questions touching our national life.
You have come to ask him to render an account of the Manitoba school question which is not settled, notwithstanding the statements of those who betrayed our bretbreu. (Mr. Normand had certainly not conferred with the hon. Minister of Public Works on the subject) and which remains to-day as it was then a glaring and monstrous violation of the natural right possessed by every man to adore God in the language spoken by bis father and mother.
You will require from Mr. Laurier and Mr. Bureau an account of their conduct at the time when contingents were sent to Africa.
How shall the hon. member whose name I cannot now mention suit to his vote on the present bill, his words as reported in 'Le Devoir' of the 6th August, 1911?
The present government (the Laurier government) do not settle great questions, they kill and bury them. (Cries of shame).
Their final method is to say of any such question that it is dead and buried.
Dead and buried indeed the Manitoba schools question notwithstanding the eloquent voice exclaiming:	I am:	the eternally
wounded and my grave is a cradle!
What does 'L'Evenement' think, or rather what should it think, being the chief organ of the conservative party in Quebec and the personal organ, as I think, of the hon. the Postmaster General, and having printed in heavy letters on the eve of the election, sentences such as this:
Let us avenge the Catholic and our fellow-countrymen of the West.
Mr. Speaker, we have witnessed and are still witnessing an ignoble comedy, a demoralizing spectacle especially when the actors are men whose first duty should be the moral and intellectual uplifting of the people; I have no doubt that the day of reckoning will come soon for those who have contributed to the gigantic farce of which we have been the unfortunate witnesses.
I do not desire to close my remarks without referring to certain statements made by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny). He told us in substance that he would not vote for the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Beauce because he had no confidence in him. His scruples should not be a matter for surprise as he has spoken to us of his conscience. But what must he think of those amongst us who supported the amendment of the hon. member for Yamaska? Does he suppose that we so voted because we had confidence in the mover, especially after the contradictory speeches delivered at two days interval by the hon. member for Yamaska? In the first he stated that after due consideration and after the dissertation of his former professor of constitutional law, he had reached the conclusion that the minority had no vested rights in Kee-watin. In the second, he discovered that the minority had vested rights. The duty of the hon. member for Dorchester is clear, there is only one matter for him to consider that is whether the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Beauce is conformable to his principles.
The hon. member for Dorchester expres-ed a regret that the hon. member for Beauce had not spoken sooner. But had he himself spoken on the question before the speech he has just delivered? As a government member his duty was to give the example. All that the hon. member for Dorchester had done before his speech delivered to-night, was to vote, as we did, for the amendment of the hon. member for Yamaska. The hon. member for Beauce, according to the logic of my friend the hon. member for Dorchester, would thus be at some advantage having spoken first.
Mr. Speaker, I shall say no more and I think that the House has already understood that I will vote in favour of the amendment of the hon. member for Beauce.

PAQUE'T (L'lslet). (Translation) Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. John and Iberville has asked me if I should continue to support the government on other political questions. I may say to him in reply that I shall always be ready to rise superior to considerations of party politics to defend leaders who best represent my views. In 1905, I defended



the rights of minorities and of the French language. I desire to do the same in regard to this ICeewatin question. In 1905, when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were being created, I joined hands notwithstanding political lines with Mr. Henri Bourassa and Mr. Armand Lavergne, in order to defend the right of minorities and of the French language in those vast prairie lands opened to civilization by our forefathers. To-day as before, in order to defend the minority rights, I am leaving for the moment those men whom I must approve and admire. My friend from Beauce comes at the last moment, comes with an amendment, asking us to vote for a conference between the government of Canada and that of Manitoba. That amendment should have come sooner. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier prepared this Bill last year he thought of no such thing. I will therefore vote with the government for the reasons given by my friend from Dorchester.
My friend from St. John has treated hon. Mr. Monk with severity. Does he not know of the patriotic spirit of the Minister of Public Works and of the efforts made by him to secure the rights of the minority? I have the greatest confidence in Mt. Monk. Never shall I forget the memorable sitting of the 3rd of February, 1910, when the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, his voice trembling from physical anguish, rose to enter his energitic protest against those who violated the rigths of minorities. I can have no confidence in the men of the Lib-al party, who endeavour to defend, when in opposition, the sacred rights of minorities betrayed by them in the past.
I left my party on this occasion in order to remain faithful to my past record; but in voting for the government against the motion of my friend from Beauce, I desire simiply to show that I have no confidence in the leaders of the Liberal party. The leaders of the Conservative party, Hon. F. D. Monk, Minister of Public Works, Hon. L. P. Pelletier and Hon. B. Nantel will know how to defend in future the true interests of Canada. I made the greatest sacrifice of my political career by voting against the government on the Keewatin schools question. Our ministers are looking towards Manitoba. I hope that they will insist upon our rights in a patriotic manner. I am sure that they will defend the true interests of the country. In so doing they deserve and will deserve my entire gratitude and confidence.

Mr. Speaker, when Manitoba was admitted into confederation there was a statutory limitation imposed with regard to education and it is the same limitation which I wanted to impose on this new territory now Mr. PAQUET.
being added to the province. Some hon. members on the other side of the House have made a distinction between creating a new province and adding territory to a province already formed. The only difference is that we must obtain the consent of the legislature of the province to the conditions or terms that we want to impose. We are treating Manitoba very generously. I think we are treating her too generously. We are giving her too much. We are in a position to impose terms and terms should be imposed. The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) is willing to trust to the mercy of Mr. Roblin and his government. Well, I am not too confident in the government of Manitoba, considering the declarations of an ex-colleague of Mr. Roblin who now sits in this House as Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers). I have here the report of a speech made by the Minister of the Interior at Virden on January 6, 1909, and it reads as follows:

Mr. Rogers, in his speech here last night, tried hard to twist the compulsory education policy which has been advocated in the legislature by the Liberals, into a sinister attack upon the educational liberties of the province made in accordance with deep-laid plans to re-establish separate schools. He declared that certain Liberals had entered into a conspiracy with Sir Wilfrid Laurier to force the issue of compulsory education, the idea being that when it reached a certain point the Dominion government would cut in and give the province the option of _ reestablishing separate schools in this province or foregoing the enlargement of its boundaries. Mr. Rogers then proceeded to deliver his time-honoured harangue upon the boundary question, displaying, - as usual, a series of maps. He represented the province as being persecuted for its devotion to the national school system; and represented Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Manitoba Liberals as engaged in a nefarious plot to compel the restoration of separate schools to the minority. This portion of Mr. Rogers' speech was a skilful and audacious appeal to feelings which are Strong in this constituency; and he closed with a fervent appeal to the electors of Virden to rally to the support of the government as defenders of the liberties of the province.
I think that the Postmaster General, when he reposes such high hopes in the Manitoba government, is living in a fool's paradise, and I think it would have been more in conformity with his duty and. especially with hijfe previous pledges and promises to his compatriots of the province of Quebec to have voted for the amendment of the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. La-marche) and to have thus safeguarded now and forever, the rights of the minority, either Catholic or Protestant, in regard to

separate schools in this new territory. I submit that the Act of 1875 has applied to the Keewatin district since the 31st January, 1907, and, moreover, I think that the ordinances 29 and 30, passed by the Northwest Territories legislature and council and which are found in the consolidated ordinances of 1901 apply to the district of Keewatin. Some hon. members on the other side of the House have maintained that the Catholics have no rights, and the Postmaster General is one of them, because there have been no separate schools in the district of Keewatin. It is true that separate schools have not been in operation, but still the right exists and they could have been organized under ordinances 29 and 30, which were in force before 1907. When the district of Keewatin became part of the Northwest Territories, those ordinances and the laws in force in the Northwest Territories became applicable and in force in the district of Keewatin. I do not intend to speak at any length at this hour, but I was anxious to explain my reasons for voting for the amendment of my hon. friend from Yamaska. I am sorry it did not carry. I would have preferred that it should have carried, but since it could not carry, since a large majority in this House was against it, I think that the best thing we can do now, is to adopt the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Bel and) and not pass this Bill before negotiations have been entered into between the province of Manitoba and the representatives of the minority in that province. The Roman Catholics of Manitoba are to meet to-morrow night. There has been a meeting called of the) Roman (Catholics from the different parts of the province. This Bill should not pass before they are heard, and before they have had an opportunity of making their representations. The law at present in force in Manitoba is not satisfactory to the Catholics. We heard the other night the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Molloy), who must know the condition of his co-religioniets in that province, say that at Winnipeg and Brandon they had to pay double taxes,- that they had to pay theiT taxes to the public schools and at the same time, they had to maintain their own schools. I do not think that the Postmaster General himself thinks that is a satisfactory condition for the Catholics of Manitoba. I think it is his duty and that of the government to leave the Bill in abeyance until a satisfactory understanding has been come to between the government of Manitoba and the Catholics of that province. I shall have very much pleasure in voting for the amendment of my hon. friend from Beauce.

Mr. Speaker, I have only one word to say upon this question which has taken up so much 1581
of the time of the House. I want to give to you, Sir, and to hon. members here present, my reasons for voting against the amendment which was proposed by the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Mondou) and in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr Baland).
I voted a few moments ago against the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Mondou), because I considered that this amendment was of a nature which rendered it either ultra vires or useless. Many legal minds have given opinions upon this school question, many eminent lawyers throughout the country have decided that it is impossible for the federal government to coerce Manitoba by the inclusion of any amendment or additional clause in this Bill without the consent of the legislature of Manitoba. I agree with these gentlemen, I agree with the opinion which was given in this House by the hon. the Minister of Justice, and that is one of the reasons which led me to vote against this amendment. It is true that it has also been stated in the course of this debate that the amendment did not have any great effect and that the principal reason why it was proposed was in order to place the new territory added to Manitoba under the same school system as the old territory. If that is the case the amendment is utterly useless because there is no doubt in my mind that the school system which exists in Manitoba at present will be extended to the new part of that province. But is that all? I claim that the hon. members who form the present government, the right hosn. the Prime Minister and his colleagues in this House, promised the people of Canada more than to give to this new territory the same school system which exists in old Manitoba. I claim that the Prime Minister indirectly and many of his ministers directly promised) the people of this country and especially of the province of Quebec that they would give separate schools to old Mianitoba, and that is what they are not doing when they present this Bill. It is very true that the Prime Minister very carefully refrained during the course of the last campaign from going into those counties in which the candidates were supposed to be of the Nationalist school and to have as their leaders Messrs. Monk and Bourassa. But he did come into Shefford and in Shefford the Prime Minister had as candidate Mr. James Davidson of Montreal who, on August 17, 1911, published a manifesto signed by his own hand which cannot be denied. In that manifesto he writes among other things:
If I am elected I will endeavour to have
the rights and prerogatives of the Catholic French Canadians of all provinces respected and recognized as are the rights of the English Protestants of the province of Quebec

with recognition of their schools, and of the French language, etc., eto.
And on August 30, or 31, the present right hon. Prime Minister addressed a meeting in Granby in favour of Mr. Davidson. Mr. Davidson was unquestionably his candidate and to-day he brings before the House a Bill in which he says not a word about separate schools. I did not vote against the amendlment proposed by the hon. member for Yamaska because I am against separate schools. I am in favour of separate schools. I think that separate schools should exist throughout the Dominion, both Catholic and Protestant; but they can only be established in Manitoba by the government of Manitoba, they cannot be forced upon that province by this government. Conferences *and conciliation, the policy of the Liberal party for the past thirty years, are the only way that improved conditions can be obtained for the minorities of Manitoba. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), .asks that a further conference be held and I believe that if ever there was a time in the history of Canada when separate schools could foe obtained from the Manitoba government, it is precisely now, when we are passing a Bill to increase the territory of Manitoba giving them thousands and thousands of square miles of territory and .millions of dollars. Now is the time to have a conference with the Prime Minister of Manitoba and to obtain from him the passage of some law in the province which would improve upon the Laurier-Greenway agreement of 1897.
Good, good!
